entries.7d7001194ccfd2f41d6c59d1ed83189eea68e103: <div sID="gen21676" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="7" osisID="Matt.7" sID="Matt.7"/> <div eID="gen21676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21677" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21678" type="x-p"/> This chapter continues and concludes Christ's sermon on the mount, which is purely practical, directing us to order our conversation aright, both toward God and man; for the design of the Christian religion is to make men good, every way good. We have, I. Some rules concerning censure and reproof, <reference osisRef="Matt.7.1-Matt.7.6">ver. 1-6</reference>. II. Encouragements given us to pray to God for what we need, <reference osisRef="Matt.7.7-Matt.7.11">ver. 7-11</reference>. III. The necessity of strictness in conversation urged upon us, <reference osisRef="Matt.7.12-Matt.7.14">ver. 12-14</reference>. IV. A caution given us to take heed of false prophets, <reference osisRef="Matt.7.15-Matt.7.20">ver. 15-20</reference>. V. The conclusion of the whole sermon, showing the necessity of universal obedience to Christ's commands, without which we cannot expect to be happy, <reference osisRef="Matt.7.21-Matt.7.27">ver. 21-27</reference>. VI. The impression which Christ's doctrine made upon his hearers, <reference osisRef="Matt.7.28-Matt.7.29">ver. 28, 29</reference>.
entries.4d96bdc57a6bd4fb82ad71a78a2fe28ffbda312a: <div eID="gen21678" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21677" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Sermon on the Mount.</title> <div sID="gen21679" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Judge not, that ye be not judged. <hi type="super">2</hi> For with what judgment ye judge, ye shall be judged: and with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again. <hi type="super">3</hi> And why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother's eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye? <hi type="super">4</hi> Or how wilt thou say to thy brother, Let me pull out the mote out of thine eye; and, behold, a beam <hi type="italic">is</hi> in thine own eye? <hi type="super">5</hi> Thou hypocrite, first cast out the beam out of thine own eye; and then shalt thou see clearly to cast out the mote out of thy brother's eye. <hi type="super">6</hi> Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you. <div eID="gen21679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21680" type="x-p"/> Our Saviour is here directing us how to conduct ourselves in reference to the faults of others; and his expressions seem intended as a reproof to the scribes and Pharisees, who were very rigid and severe, very magisterial and supercilious, in condemning all about them, as those commonly are, that are proud and conceited in justifying themselves. We have here, <div eID="gen21680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21681" type="x-p"/> I. A caution <hi type="italic">against judging</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.7.1-Matt.7.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. There are those whose office it is to judge-magistrates and ministers. Christ, though he made not himself a Judge, yet came not to unmake them, for by him <hi type="italic">princes decree justice;</hi> but this is directed to private persons, to his disciples, who shall hereafter <hi type="italic">sit on thrones judging,</hi> but not now. Now observe, <div eID="gen21681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21682" type="x-p"/> 1. The prohibition; <hi type="italic">Judge not.</hi> We must judge ourselves, and judge our own acts, but we must not judge our brother, not magisterially assume such an authority over others, as we allow not them over us: since our rule is, to be <hi type="italic">subject to one another.</hi> <hi type="italic">Be not many masters,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.3.1">Jam. iii. 1</reference>. We must not sit in the judgment-seat, to make our word a law to every body. We must not judge our brother, that is, we must not <hi type="italic">speak evil</hi> of him, so it is explained, <reference osisRef="Jas.4.11">Jam. iv. 11</reference>. We must not <hi type="italic">despise him,</hi> nor <hi type="italic">set him at nought,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.14.10">Rom. xiv. 10</reference>. We must not judge rashly, nor pass such a judgment upon our brother as has no ground, but is only the product of our own jealousy and ill nature. We must not make the worst of people, nor infer such invidious things from their words and actions as they will not bear. We must not judge uncharitably, unmercifully, nor with a spirit of revenge, and a desire to do mischief. We must not judge of a man's state by a single act, nor of what he is in himself by what he is to us, because in our own cause we are apt to be partial. We must not judge the hearts of others, nor their intentions, for it is God's prerogative to try the heart, and we must not step into his throne; nor must we judge of their eternal state, nor call them <hi type="italic">hypocrites, reprobates,</hi> and <hi type="italic">castaways;</hi> that is stretching beyond our line; what have we to do, thus to judge another man's servant? Counsel him, and help him, but do not judge him. <div eID="gen21682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21683" type="x-p"/> 2. The reason to enforce this prohibition. <hi type="italic">That ye be not judged.</hi> This intimates, (1.) That if we presume to judge others, we may expect to be ourselves judged. He who usurps the bench, shall be called to the bar; he shall be judged of men; commonly none are more censured, than those who are most censorious; every one will have a stone to throw at them; he who, like Ishmael, has his hand, his tongue, <hi type="italic">against every man,</hi> shall, like him, have <hi type="italic">every man's</hi> hand and tongue <hi type="italic">against him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.16.12">Gen. xvi. 12</reference>); and no mercy shall be shown to the reputation of those that show no mercy to the reputation of others. Yet that is not the worst of it; they shall be judged of God; from him they shall receive the <hi type="italic">greater condemnation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.3.1">Jam. iii. 1</reference>. Both parties must appear before him (<reference osisRef="Rom.14.10">Rom. xiv. 10</reference>), who, as he will relieve the <hi type="italic">humble sufferer,</hi> will also resist the <hi type="italic">haughty scorner,</hi> and give him enough of judging. (2.) That if we be modest and charitable in our censures of others, and decline judging them, and judge ourselves rather, <hi type="italic">we shall not be judged of the Lord.</hi> As God will forgive those that forgive their brethren; so he will not judge those that will not judge their brethren; the <hi type="italic">merciful shall find mercy.</hi> It is an evidence of humility, charity, and deference to God, and shall be owned and rewarded by him accordingly. See <reference osisRef="Rom.14.10">Rom. xiv. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen21683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21684" type="x-p"/> The judging of those that judge others is according to the law of retaliation; <hi type="italic">With what judgment ye judge, ye shall be judged,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.7.2">v. 2</reference>. The righteous God, in his judgments, often observes a rule of proportion, as in the case of Adonibezek, <reference osisRef="Judg.1.7">Judg. i. 7</reference>. See also <reference osisRef="Rev.13.10">Rev. xiii. 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.18.6">xviii. 6</reference>. Thus will he be both justified and magnified in his judgments, and all flesh will be silenced before him. <hi type="italic">With what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again;</hi> perhaps in this world, so that men may read their sin in their punishment. Let this deter us from all severity in dealing with our brother. <hi type="italic">What shall we do when God rises up?</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.31.14">Job xxxi. 14</reference>. What would become of us, if God should be as exact and severe in judging us, as we are in judging our brethren; if he should weigh us in the same balance? We may justly expect it, if we be extreme to mark what our brethren do amiss. In this, as in other things, the violent dealings of men return upon their own heads. <div eID="gen21684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21685" type="x-p"/> II. Some cautions <hi type="italic">about reproving.</hi> Because we must not judge others, which is a great sin, it does not therefore follow that we must not reprove others, which is a great duty, and may be a means of <hi type="italic">saving a soul from death;</hi> however, it will be a means of saving our souls from sharing in their guilt. Now observe here, <div eID="gen21685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21686" type="x-p"/> 1. It is not every one who is fit to reprove. Those who are themselves guilty of the same faults of which they accuse others, or of worse, bring shame upon themselves, and are not likely to do good to those whom they reprove, <reference osisRef="Matt.7.3-Matt.7.5">v. 3-5</reference>. Here is, <div eID="gen21686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21687" type="x-p"/> (1.) A just reproof to the censorious, who quarrel with their brother for small faults, while they allow themselves in great ones; who are quick-sighted to spy <hi type="italic">a mote</hi> in his eye, but are not sensible of <hi type="italic">a beam in their own;</hi> nay, and will be very officious to <hi type="italic">pull out the mote out of his eye,</hi> when they are as unfit to do it as if they were themselves quite blind. Note, [1.] There are degrees in sin: some sins are comparatively but as <hi type="italic">motes,</hi> others as <hi type="italic">beams;</hi> some as a <hi type="italic">gnat,</hi> others as a <hi type="italic">camel:</hi> not that there is any sin little, for there is no little God to sin against; if it be a <hi type="italic">mote</hi> (or <hi type="italic">splinter,</hi> for so it might better be read), it is in the eye; if a <hi type="italic">gnat,</hi> it is in the throat; both painful and perilous, and we cannot be easy or well till they are got out. [2.] Our own sins ought to appear greater to us than the same sins in others: that which charity teaches us to call but a <hi type="italic">splinter in our brother's eye,</hi> true repentance and godly sorrow will teach us to call a <hi type="italic">beam in our own;</hi> for the sins of others must be extenuated, but our own aggravated. [3.] There are many that have <hi type="italic">beams in their own eyes,</hi> and yet do not consider it. They are under the guilt and dominion of very great sins, and yet are not aware of it, but justify themselves, as if they needed no repentance nor reformation; it is as strange that a man can be in such a sinful, miserable condition, and not be aware of it, as that a man should have a beam in him eye, and not consider it; but the god of this world so artfully blinds their minds, that notwithstanding, with great assurance, they say, <hi type="italic">We see.</hi> [4.] It is common for those who are most sinful themselves, and least sensible of it, to be most forward and free in judging and censuring others: the Pharisees, who were most haughty in justifying themselves, were most scornful in condemning others. They were severe upon Christ's disciples for <hi type="italic">eating with unwashen hands,</hi> which was scarcely a <hi type="italic">mote,</hi> while they encouraged men in a contempt of their parents, which was a <hi type="italic">beam.</hi> Pride and uncharitableness are commonly <hi type="italic">beams</hi> in the eyes of those that pretend to be critical and nice in their censures of others. Nay, many are guilty of that secret, which they have the face to punish in others when it is discovered. <hi type="italic">Cogita tecum, fortasse vitium de quo quereris, si te diligenter excusseris, in sinu invenies; inique publico irasceris crimini tuo—Reflect that perhaps the fault of which you complain, might, on a strict examination, be discovered in yourself; and that it would be unjust publicly to express indignation against your own crime.</hi> Seneca, <hi type="italic">de Beneficiis.</hi> But, [5.] Men's being so severe upon the faults of others, while they are indulgent of their own, is a mark of hypocrisy. <hi type="italic">Thou hypocrite,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.7.5">v. 5</reference>. Whatever such a one may pretend, it is certain that he is no enemy to sin (if he were, he would be an enemy to his own sin), and therefore he is not worthy of praise; nay, it appears that he is an enemy to his brother, and therefore worthy of blame. This spiritual charity must begin at home; "<hi type="italic">For how canst thou say,</hi> how canst thou for shame say, to thy brother, <hi type="italic">Let me help to reform thee,</hi> when thou takest no care to reform thyself? Thy own heart will upbraid thee with the absurdity of it; thou wilt do it with an ill grace, and thou wilt expect every one to tell thee, that <hi type="italic">vice corrects sin: physician, heal thyself;" I præ, sequar—Go you before, I will follow.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Rom.2.21">Rom. ii. 21</reference>. [6.] The consideration of what is amiss in ourselves, though it ought not to keep us from administering friendly reproof, ought to keep us from magisterial censuring, and to make us very candid and charitable in judging others. "Therefore <hi type="italic">restore with the spirit of meekness, considering thyself</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gal.6.1">Gal. vi. 1</reference>); what thou has been, what thou art, and what thou wouldst be, if God should leave thee to thyself." <div eID="gen21687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21688" type="x-p"/> (2.) Here is a good rule for reprovers, <reference osisRef="Matt.7.5">v. 5</reference>. Go in the right method, <hi type="italic">first cast the beam out of thine own eye.</hi> Our own badness is so far from excusing us in not reproving, that our being by it rendered unfit to reprove is an aggravation of our badness; I must not say, "I have <hi type="italic">a beam in my own eye,</hi> and therefore I will not help my brother with the <hi type="italic">mote out of his.</hi>" A man's <hi type="italic">of</hi>fence will never be his <hi type="italic">de</hi>fence: but I must first reform myself, that I may thereby help to reform my brother, and may qualify myself to reprove him. Note, Those who blame others, ought to be blameless and harmless themselves. Those who are <hi type="italic">reprovers in the gate,</hi> reprovers by office, magistrates and ministers, are concerned to <hi type="italic">walk circumspectly,</hi> and to be very regular in their conversation: an <hi type="italic">elder must have a good report,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.2">1 Tim. iii. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.7">7</reference>. The snuffers of the sanctuary were to be of pure gold. <div eID="gen21688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21689" type="x-p"/> 2. It is not every one that is fit to be reproved; <hi type="italic">Give not that which is holy unto the dogs,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.7.6">v. 6</reference>. This may be considered, either, (1.) As a rule to the disciples in preaching the gospel; not that they must not preach it to any one who were wicked and profane (Christ himself preached to publicans and sinners), but the reference is to such as they found obstinate after the gospel was preached to them, such as blasphemed it, and persecuted the preachers of it; let them not spend much time among such, for it would be lost labour, but let them turn to others, <reference osisRef="Acts.13.41">Acts xiii. 41</reference>. So Dr. Whitby. Or, (2.) As a rule to all in giving reproof. Our zeal against sin must be guided by discretion, and we must not go about to give instructions, counsels, and rebukes, much less comforts, to hardened scorners, to whom it will certainly do no good, but who will be exasperated and enraged at us. Throw a pearl to a swine, and he will resent it, as if you threw a stone at him; <hi type="italic">reproofs</hi> will be called <hi type="italic">reproaches,</hi> as they were (<reference osisRef="Luke.11.45">Luke xi. 45</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.6.10">Jer. vi. 10</reference>), therefore give not to dogs and swine (unclean creatures) holy things. Note, [1.] Good counsel and reproof are a holy thing, and a pearl: they are ordinances of God, they are precious; as an <hi type="italic">ear-ring of gold, and an ornament of fine gold,</hi> so is the wise reprover (<reference osisRef="Prov.25.12">Prov. xxv. 12</reference>), and a wise reproof is <hi type="italic">like an excellent oil</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.141.5">Ps. cxli. 5</reference>); it is <hi type="italic">a tree of life</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.18">Prov. iii. 18</reference>). [2.] Among the generation of the wicked, there are some that have arrived at such a pitch of wickedness, that they are looked upon as dogs and swine; they are impudently and notoriously vile; they have so long <hi type="italic">walked in the way of sinners,</hi> that they have sat down <hi type="italic">in the seat of the scornful;</hi> they professedly hate and despise instruction, and set it at defiance, so that they are irrecoverably and irreclaimably wicked; they return with <hi type="italic">the dog to his vomit,</hi> and with the <hi type="italic">sow to her wallowing in the mire.</hi> [3.] Reproofs of instruction are ill bestowed upon such, and expose the reprover to all the contempt and mischief that may be expected from dogs and swine. One can expect no other than that they will trample the reproofs under their feet, in scorn of them, and rage against them; for they are impatient of control and contradiction; and they will turn again and rend the reprovers; rend their good names with their revilings, return them wounding words for their healing ones; rend them with persecution; Herod rent John Baptist for his faithfulness. See here what is the evidence of men's being <hi type="italic">dogs</hi> and <hi type="italic">swine.</hi> Those are to be reckoned such, who <hi type="italic">hate reproofs</hi> and reprovers, and fly in the face of those who, in kindness to their souls, show them their sin and danger. These sin against the remedy; who shall heal and help those that will not be healed and helped? It is plain that God has determined to destroy such. <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.16">2 Chron. xxv. 16</reference>. The rule here given is applicable to the distinguishing, sealing ordinances of the gospel; which must not be prostituted to those who are openly wicked and profane, lest holy things be thereby rendered contemptible, and unholy persons be thereby hardened. <hi type="italic">It is not meet to take the children's bread, and cast it to the dogs.</hi> Yet we must be very cautious whom we condemn as dogs and swine, and not do it till after trial, and upon full evidence. Many a patient is lost, by being thought to be so, who, if means had been used, might have been saved. As we must take heed of calling the <hi type="italic">good,</hi> <hi type="italic">bad,</hi> by judging all professors to be hypocrites; so we must take heed of calling the <hi type="italic">bad,</hi> <hi type="italic">desperate,</hi> by judging all the wicked to be <hi type="italic">dogs</hi> and <hi type="italic">swine.</hi> [4.] Our Lord Jesus is very tender of the safety of his people, and would not have them needlessly to expose themselves to the fury of those that will <hi type="italic">turn again and rend</hi> them. Let them not be <hi type="italic">righteous over much,</hi> so as to destroy themselves. Christ makes the law of self-preservation one of his own laws, and <hi type="italic">precious is the blood</hi> of his subjects to him.
entries.3f6b20cbb3c8bc8065454bc565b60c31a3cd0a74: <div eID="gen21689" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Sermon on the Mount.</title> <div sID="gen21690" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you: <hi type="super">8</hi> For every one that asketh receiveth; and he that seeketh findeth; and to him that knocketh it shall be opened. <hi type="super">9</hi> Or what man is there of you, whom if his son ask bread, will he give him a stone? 10 Or if he ask a fish, will he give him a serpent? <hi type="super">11</hi> If ye then, being evil, know how to give good gifts unto your children, how much more shall your Father which is in heaven give good things to them that ask him? <div eID="gen21690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21691" type="x-p"/> Our Saviour, in the foregoing chapter, had spoken of prayer as a commanded duty, by which God is honoured, and which, if done aright, shall be rewarded; here he speaks of it as the appointed means of obtaining what we need, especially grace to obey the precepts he had given, some of which are so displeasing to flesh and blood. <div eID="gen21691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21692" type="x-p"/> I. Here is a precept in three words to the same purport, <hi type="italic">Ask, Seek, Knock</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.7.7">v. 7</reference>); that is, in one word, "Pray; pray often; pray with sincerity and seriousness; pray, and pray again; make conscience of prayer, and be constant in it; make a business of prayer, and be earnest in it. <hi type="italic">Ask,</hi> as a beggar asks alms." Those that would be rich in grace, must betake themselves to the poor trade of begging, and they shall find it a thriving trade. "<hi type="italic">Ask;</hi> represent your wants and burthens to God, and refer yourselves to him for support and supply, according to his promise. <hi type="italic">Ask</hi> as a traveller asks the way; to pray is to <hi type="italic">enquire of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.37">Ezek. xxxvi. 37</reference>. <hi type="italic">Seek,</hi> as for a thing of value that we have lost, or as the merchantman that <hi type="italic">seeks goodly pearls.</hi> <hi type="italic">Seek by prayer,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.9.3">Dan. ix. 3</reference>. <hi type="italic">Knock,</hi> as he that desires to enter into the house knocks at the door." We would be admitted to converse with God, would be taken into his love, and favour, and kingdom; sin has shut and barred the door against us; by prayer, we knock; <hi type="italic">Lord, Lord, open to us.</hi> Christ knocks at our door (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.20">Rev. iii. 20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Song.5.2">Cant. v. 2</reference>); and allows us to knock at his, which is a favour we do not allow to common beggars. Seeking and knocking imply something more than asking and praying. 1. We must not only <hi type="italic">ask</hi> but <hi type="italic">seek;</hi> we must second our prayers with our endeavors; we must, in the use of the appointed means, <hi type="italic">seek</hi> for that which we <hi type="italic">ask</hi> for, else we tempt God. When the dresser of the vineyard asked for a year's respite for the barren fig-tree, he added, <hi type="italic">I will dig about it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.13.7-Luke.13.8">Luke xiii. 7, 8</reference>. God gives knowledge and grace to those that search the scriptures, and wait at Wisdom's gates; and power against sin to those that avoid the occasions of it. 2. We must not only <hi type="italic">ask,</hi> but <hi type="italic">knock;</hi> we must come to God's door, must <hi type="italic">ask</hi> importunately; not only pray, but plead and wrestle with God; we must <hi type="italic">seek</hi> diligently; we must continue knocking; must persevere in prayer, and in the use of means; must endure to the end in the duty. <div eID="gen21692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21693" type="x-p"/> II. Here is a promised annexed: <hi type="italic">our labour</hi> in prayer, if indeed we do labour in it, <hi type="italic">shall not be in vain:</hi> where God finds a praying heart, he will be found a prayer-hearing God; <hi type="italic">he shall give thee an answer of peace.</hi> The precept is threefold, <hi type="italic">ask, seek, knock;</hi> there is <hi type="italic">precept upon precept;</hi> but the promise is sixfold, <hi type="italic">line upon line,</hi> for our encouragement; because a firm belief of the promise would make us cheerful and constant in our obedience. Now here, <div eID="gen21693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21694" type="x-p"/> 1. The promise is made, and made so as exactly to answer the precept, <reference osisRef="Matt.7.7">v. 7</reference>. <hi type="italic">Ask, and it shall be given you;</hi> not lent you, not sold you, but <hi type="italic">given you;</hi> and what is more free than gift? Whatever you pray for, according to the promise, whatever you <hi type="italic">ask, shall be given you,</hi> if God see it fit for you, and what would you have more? It is but <hi type="italic">ask</hi> and have; <hi type="italic">ye have not, because ye ask not,</hi> or <hi type="italic">ask</hi> not aright: what is not worth asking, is not worth having, and then it is worth nothing. <hi type="italic">Seek,</hi> and <hi type="italic">ye shall find,</hi> and then you do not lose your labour; God is himself <hi type="italic">found of those that seek</hi> him, and if we find him we have enough. "<hi type="italic">Knock, and it shall be opened;</hi> the door of mercy and grace shall no longer be shut against you as enemies and intruders, but opened to you as friends and children. It will be asked, <hi type="italic">who is at the door?</hi> If you be able to say, a friend, and have the ticket of promise ready to produce in the hand of faith, doubt not of admission. If the door be not <hi type="italic">opened</hi> at the first <hi type="italic">knock, continue instant in prayer;</hi> it is an affront to a friend to <hi type="italic">knock</hi> at his door, and then go away; though he tarry, yet wait." <div eID="gen21694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21695" type="x-p"/> 2. It is repeated, <reference osisRef="Matt.7.8">v. 8</reference>. It is to the same purport, yet with some addition. (1.) It is made to extend to all that pray aright; "Not only you my disciples shall receive what you pray for, but <hi type="italic">every one that asketh, receiveth,</hi> whether Jew or Gentile, young or old, rich or poor, high or low, master or servant, learned or unlearned, they are all alike welcome to <hi type="italic">the throne of grace,</hi> if they come in faith: <hi type="italic">for God is no respecter of persons.</hi>" (2.) It is made so as to amount to a grant, in words of the present tense, which is more than a promise for the future. <hi type="italic">Every one that asketh,</hi> not only <hi type="italic">shall</hi> receive, but <hi type="italic">receiveth;</hi> by faith, applying and appropriating the promise, we are actually interested and invested in the good promised: so sure and inviolable are the promises of God, that they do, in effect, give present possession: an active believer enters immediately, and makes the blessings promised his own. What have we in hope, according to the promise, is as sure, and should be as sweet, as what we have in hand. <hi type="italic">God hath spoken in his holiness,</hi> and then <hi type="italic">Gilead is mine, Manasseh mine</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.108.7-Ps.108.8">Ps. cviii. 7, 8</reference>); it is all mine own, if I can but make it so by believing it so. Conditional grants become absolute upon the performance of the condition; so here, <hi type="italic">he that asketh, receiveth.</hi> Christ hereby puts his <hi type="italic">fiat</hi> to the petition; and he having all power, that is enough. <div eID="gen21695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21696" type="x-p"/> 3. It is illustrated, by a similitude taken from earthly parents, and their innate readiness to give their children what they ask. Christ appeals to his hearers, <hi type="italic">What man is there of you,</hi> though never so morose and ill-humoured, <hi type="italic">whom if his son ask bread, will he give him a stone?</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.7.9-Matt.7.10">v. 9, 10</reference>. Whence he infers (<reference osisRef="Matt.7.11">v. 11</reference>), <hi type="italic">If ye then, being evil,</hi> yet grant your children's requests, <hi type="italic">much more will your heavenly Father give you the good things you ask.</hi> Now this is of use, <div eID="gen21696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21697" type="x-p"/> (1.) To <hi type="italic">direct</hi> our prayers and expectations. [1.] We must come to God, as children to a <hi type="italic">Father in heaven,</hi> with reverence and confidence. How naturally does a child in want or distress run to the father with its complaints; <hi type="italic">My head, my head;</hi> thus should the new nature send us to God for supports and supplies. [2.] We must come to him for <hi type="italic">good things,</hi> for those he <hi type="italic">gives to them that ask him;</hi> which teaches us to refer ourselves to him; we know not what is good for ourselves (<reference osisRef="Eccl.6.12">Eccl. vi. 12</reference>), but he knows what is good for us, we must therefore leave it with him; <hi type="italic">Father, thy will be done.</hi> The child is here supposed to <hi type="italic">ask bread,</hi> that is necessary, and <hi type="italic">a fish,</hi> that is wholesome; but if the child should foolishly ask for <hi type="italic">a stone,</hi> or <hi type="italic">a serpent,</hi> for unripe fruit to eat, or a sharp knife to play with, the father, though kind, is so wise as to deny him. We often ask that of God which would do us harm if we had it; he knows this, and therefore does not give it to us. Denials in love are better than grants in anger; we should have been undone ere this if we had had all we desired; this is admirably well expressed by a heathen, Juvenal, <hi type="italic">Sat.</hi> 10. <div eID="gen21697" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen21698"/> <l level="1" sID="gen21699"/><hi type="italic">Permittes ipsis expendere numinibus, quid</hi><l eID="gen21699" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen21700"/><hi type="italic">Conveniat nobis, rebusque sit utile nostris,</hi><l eID="gen21700" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen21701"/><hi type="italic">Nam pro jucundis aptissima quæque dabunt dii.</hi><l eID="gen21701" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen21702"/><hi type="italic">Carior est illis homo, quam sibi: nos animorum</hi><l eID="gen21702" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen21703"/><hi type="italic">Impulsu, et cæca, magnaque cupidine ducti,</hi><l eID="gen21703" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen21704"/><hi type="italic">Conjugium petimus, partumque uxoris; at illis</hi><l eID="gen21704" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen21705"/><hi type="italic">Notum est, qui pueri, qualisque futura sit uxor.</hi><l eID="gen21705" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen21706"/>Entrust thy fortune to the powers above.<l eID="gen21706" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen21707"/>Leave them to manage for thee, and to grant<l eID="gen21707" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen21708"/>What their unerring wisdom sees thee want:<l eID="gen21708" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen21709"/>In goodness, as in greatness, they excel;<l eID="gen21709" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen21710"/>Ah, that we lov'd ourselves but half so well!<l eID="gen21710" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen21711"/>We, blindly by our headstrong passions led,<l eID="gen21711" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen21712"/>Seek a companion, and desire to wed;<l eID="gen21712" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen21713"/>Then wish for heirs: but to the gods alone<l eID="gen21713" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen21714"/>Our future offspring and our wives are known.<l eID="gen21714" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen21698"/> <div sID="gen21715" type="x-p"/> (2.) To <hi type="italic">encourage</hi> our prayers and expectations. We may hope that we shall not be denied and disappointed: we shall not have <hi type="italic">a stone</hi> for <hi type="italic">bread,</hi> to break our teeth (though we have a hard crust to employ our teeth), nor <hi type="italic">a serpent</hi> for <hi type="italic">a fish,</hi> to sting us; we have reason indeed to fear it, because we deserve it, but God will be better to us than the desert of our sins. The world often gives <hi type="italic">stones for bread,</hi> and <hi type="italic">serpents for fish,</hi> but God never does; nay, we shall be heard and answered, for children are by their parents. [1.] God has put into the hearts of parents a compassionate inclination to succour and supply their children, according to their need. Even those that have had little conscience of duty, yet have done it, as it were by instinct. No law was ever thought necessary to oblige parents to maintain their legitimate children, nor, in Solomon's time, their illegitimate ones. [2.] He has assumed the relation of a Father to us, and owns us for his children; that from the readiness we find in ourselves to relieve our children, we may be encouraged to apply ourselves to him for relief. What love and tenderness fathers have are from him; not from nature but from the God of nature; and therefore they must needs be infinitely greater in himself. He compares his concern for his people to that of a father for his children (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.13">Ps. ciii. 13</reference>), nay, to that of a mother, which is usually more tender, <reference osisRef="Isa.66.13">Isa. lxvi. 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.49.14-Isa.49.15">xlix. 14, 15</reference>. But here it is supposed, that his love, and tenderness, and goodness, far excel that of any earthly parent; and therefore it is argued with a <hi type="italic">much more,</hi> and it is grounded upon this undoubted truth, that God is a better Father, infinitely better than any earthly parents are; <hi type="italic">his thoughts are above theirs.</hi> Our earthly fathers have taken care of us; we have taken care of our children; much more will God take care of his; for they are evil, originally so; the degenerate seed of fallen Adam; they have lost much of the good nature that belonged to humanity, and among other corruptions, have that of crossness and unkindness in them; yet they <hi type="italic">give good things to their children,</hi> and they <hi type="italic">know how to give,</hi> suitably and seasonably; <hi type="italic">much more will</hi> God, for he takes up when they forsake, <reference osisRef="Ps.27.10">Ps. xxvii. 10</reference>. And, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> God is more knowing; parents are often foolishly fond, but God is wise, infinitely so; he knows what we need, what we desire, and what is fit for us. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> God is more kind. If all the compassions of all the tender fathers in the world were crowded into the bowels of one, yet compared <hi type="italic">with the tender mercies of our God,</hi> they would be but as a candle to the sun, or a drop to the ocean. God is more rich, and more ready to give to his children than the fathers of our flesh can be; for he is the Father of our spirits, an ever-loving, ever-living Father. The bowels of Fathers yearn even towards undutiful children, towards prodigals, as David's toward Absalom, and will not all this serve to silence disbelief?
entries.8a0c4511b9d807d3bdef0a0970f4a90ef9abc6a4: <div eID="gen21715" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Sermon on the Mount.</title> <div sID="gen21716" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them: for this is the law and the prophets. <hi type="super">13</hi> Enter ye in at the strait gate: for wide <hi type="italic">is</hi> the gate, and broad <hi type="italic">is</hi> the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat: <hi type="super">14</hi> Because strait <hi type="italic">is</hi> the gate, and narrow <hi type="italic">is</hi> the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it. <div eID="gen21716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21717" type="x-p"/> Our Lord Jesus here presses upon us that righteousness towards men which is an essential branch of true religion, and that religion towards God which is an essential branch of universal righteousness. <div eID="gen21717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21718" type="x-p"/> I. We must make righteousness our rule, and be ruled by it, <reference osisRef="Matt.7.12">v. 12</reference>. <hi type="italic">Therefore,</hi> lay this down for your principle, to do as you would be done by; therefore, that you may conform to the foregoing precepts, which are particular, that you may not judge and censure others, go by this rule in general; (you would not be censured, therefore do not censure), Or that you may have the benefit of the foregoing promises. Fitly is the law of justice subjoined to the law of prayer, for unless we be honest in our conversation, God will not hear our prayers, <reference osisRef="Isa.1.15-Isa.1.17">Isa. i. 15-17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.58.6-Isa.58.9">lviii. 6, 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.7.9 Zech.7.13">Zech. vii. 9, 13</reference>. We cannot expect to receive <hi type="italic">good things</hi> from God, if we do not <hi type="italic">fair</hi> things, and that which is <hi type="italic">honest,</hi> and <hi type="italic">lovely, and of good report</hi> among men. We must not only be devout, but honest, else our devotion is but hypocrisy. Now here we have, <div eID="gen21718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21719" type="x-p"/> 1. The rule of justice laid down; <hi type="italic">Whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do you even so to them.</hi> Christ came to teach us, not only what we are to know and believe, but what we are to do; what we are to do, not only toward God, but toward men; not only towards our fellow-disciples, those of our party and persuasion, but towards men in general, all with whom we have to do. The golden rule of equity is, to do to others as we would they should do to us. Alexander Severus, a heathen emperor, was a great admirer of this rule, had it written upon the walls of his closet, often quoted it in giving judgment, honoured Christ, and favoured Christians for the sake of it. <hi type="italic">Quod tibi, hoc alteri—do to others as you would they should do to you.</hi> Take it negatively (<hi type="italic">Quod tibi fieri non vis, ne alteri feceris</hi>), or positively, it comes all to the same. We must not do to others the evil they have done us, nor the evil which they would do to us, if it were in their power; nor may we do that which we think, if it were done to us, we could bear contentedly, but what we desire should be done to us. This is grounded upon that great commandment, <hi type="italic">Thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself.</hi> As we must bear the same affection to our neighbour that we would have borne to ourselves, so we must do the same good offices. The meaning of this rule lies in three things. (1.) We must do that to our neighbour which we ourselves acknowledge to be fit and reasonable: the appeal is made to our own judgment, and the discovery of our judgment is referred to that which is our own will and expectation, when it is our own case. (2.) We must put other people upon the level with ourselves, and reckon we are as much obliged to them, as they to us. We are as much bound to the duty of justice as they, and they as much entitled to the benefit of it as we. (3.) We must, in our dealings with men, suppose ourselves in the same particular case and circumstances with those we have to do with, and deal accordingly. If I were making such a one's bargain, labouring under such a one's infirmity and affliction, how should I desire and expect to be treated? And this is a just supposition, because we know not how soon their case may really be ours: at least we may fear, lest God by his judgments should do to us as we have done to others, if we have not done as we would be done by. <div eID="gen21719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21720" type="x-p"/> 2. A reason given to enforce this rule; <hi type="italic">This is the law and the prophets.</hi> It is the summary of that second great commandment, which is one of the two, <hi type="italic">on which hang all the law and the prophets,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.22.40">ch. xxii. 40</reference>. We have not this in so many words, either in <hi type="italic">the law</hi> or <hi type="italic">the prophets,</hi> but it is the concurring language of the whole. All that is there said concerning our duty towards our neighbour (and that is no little) may be reduced to this rule. Christ has here adopted it into this law; so that both the Old Testament and the New agree in prescribing this to us, to do as we would be done by. By this rule the law of Christ is commended, but the lives of Christians are condemned by comparing them with it. <hi type="italic">Aut hoc non evangelium, authi non evangelici.—Either this is not the gospel, or these are not Christians.</hi> <div eID="gen21720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21721" type="x-p"/> II. We must make religion our business, and be intent upon it; we must be strict and circumspect in our conversation, which is here represented to us as entering in at a <hi type="italic">strait gate,</hi> and walking on in a <hi type="italic">narrow way,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.7.13-Matt.7.14">v. 13, 14</reference>. Observe here, <div eID="gen21721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21722" type="x-p"/> 1. The account that is given of the bad way of sin, and the good way of holiness. There are but two ways, right and wrong, good and evil; the way to heaven, and the way to hell; in the one of which we are all of us walking: no middle place hereafter, no middle way now: the distinction of the children of men into saints and sinners, godly and ungodly, will swallow up all to eternity. <div eID="gen21722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21723" type="x-p"/> Here is, (1.) An account given us of the way of sin and sinners; both what is the best, and what is the worst of it. <div eID="gen21723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21724" type="x-p"/> [1.] That which allures multitudes into it, and keeps them in it; <hi type="italic">the gate is wide, and the way broad,</hi> and there are many travellers in that way. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> "You will have abundance of liberty in that way; <hi type="italic">the gate is wide,</hi> and stands wide open to tempt those that go right on their way. You may go in at this gate with all your lusts about you; it gives no check to your appetites, to your passions: you may <hi type="italic">walk in the way of your heart, and in the sight of your eyes;</hi> that gives room enough." It is a <hi type="italic">broad way,</hi> for there is nothing to hedge in those that walk in it, but they wander endlessly; a <hi type="italic">broad way,</hi> for there are many paths in it; there is choice of sinful ways, contrary to each other, but all paths in this <hi type="italic">broad way.</hi> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> "You will have abundance of company in that way: <hi type="italic">many there be that go in</hi> at this gate, and walk in this way." If we <hi type="italic">follow the multitude,</hi> it will be <hi type="italic">to do evil:</hi> if we go with the crowd, it will be the wrong way. It is natural for us to incline to go down the stream, and do as the most do; but it is too great a compliment, to be willing to be damned for company, and to go to hell with them, because they will not go to heaven with us: if many perish, we should be the more cautious. <div eID="gen21724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21725" type="x-p"/> [2.] That which should affright us all from it is, that it <hi type="italic">leads to destruction.</hi> Death, eternal death, is at the end of it (and the way of sin tends to it),—everlasting <hi type="italic">destruction from the presence of the Lord.</hi> Whether it be the high way of open profaneness, or the back way of close hypocrisy, if it be a way of sin, it will be our ruin, if we repent not. <div eID="gen21725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21726" type="x-p"/> (2.) Here is an account given us of the way of holiness. <div eID="gen21726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21727" type="x-p"/> [1.] What there is in it that frightens many from it; let us know the worst of it, that we may sit down and count the cost. Christ deals faithfully with us, and tells us, <div eID="gen21727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21728" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That <hi type="italic">the gate is strait.</hi> Conversion and regeneration are <hi type="italic">the gate,</hi> by which we enter into this way, in which we begin a life of faith and serious godliness; out of a state of sin into a state of grace we must pass, by the new birth, <reference osisRef="John.3.3">John iii. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.3.5">5</reference>. This is a <hi type="italic">strait gate,</hi> hard to find, and hard to get through; like a passage between two rocks, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.4">1 Sam. xiv. 4</reference>. There must be <hi type="italic">a new heart, and a new spirit,</hi> and <hi type="italic">old things must pass away.</hi> The bent of the soul must be changed, corrupt habits and customs broken off; what we have been doing all our days must be undone again. We must swim against the stream; much opposition must be struggled with, and broken through, from without, and from within. It is easier to set a man against all the world than against himself, and yet this must be in conversion. It is a <hi type="italic">strait gate,</hi> for we must stoop, or we cannot go in at it; we must become as little children; high thoughts must be brought down; nay, we must strip, must deny ourselves, put off the world, <hi type="italic">put off the old man;</hi> we must be willing to forsake all for our interest in Christ. <hi type="italic">The gate is strait</hi> to all, but to some straiter than others; as to the rich, to some that have been long prejudiced against religion. <hi type="italic">The gate is strait;</hi> blessed be God, it is not shut up, nor locked against us, nor kept with a flaming sword, as it will be shortly, <reference osisRef="Matt.25.10">ch. xxv. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen21728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21729" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That <hi type="italic">the way is narrow.</hi> We are not in heaven as soon as we have got through the <hi type="italic">strait gate,</hi> nor in Canaan as soon as we have got through the Red Sea; no, we must go through a wilderness, must travel a <hi type="italic">narrow way,</hi> hedged in by the divine law, which <hi type="italic">is exceedingly broad,</hi> and that makes <hi type="italic">the way narrow;</hi> self must be denied, the body kept under, corruptions mortified, that are as a <hi type="italic">right eye</hi> and a <hi type="italic">right hand;</hi> daily temptations must be resisted; duties must be done that are against our inclination. We must endure hardness, must wrestle and be in an agony, must watch in all things, and walk with care and circumspection. We must go <hi type="italic">through much tribulation.</hi> It is <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">hodos tethlimmene</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">an afflicted way,</hi> a way hedged about with thorns; blessed be God, it is not hedged up. The bodies we carry about with us, and the corruptions remaining in us, make the way of our duty difficult; but, as the understanding and will grow more and more sound, it will open and enlarge, and grow more and more pleasant. <div eID="gen21729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21730" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Thirdly, The gate</hi> being so <hi type="italic">strait and the way so narrow,</hi> it is not strange that there are but <hi type="italic">few that find it,</hi> and choose it. Many pass it by, through carelessness; they will not be at the pains to find it; they are well as they are, and see no need to change their way. Others look upon it, but shun it; they like not to be so limited and restrained. Those that are going to heaven are but few, compared to those that are going to hell; a remnant, a little flock, like the grape-gleanings of the vintage; as the eight that were saved in the ark, <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.20">1 Pet. iii. 20</reference>. <hi type="italic">In vitia alter alterum trudimus; Quomodo ad salutem revocari potest, quum nullus retrahit, et populus impellit—In the ways of vice men urge each other onward: how shall any one be restored to the path of safety, when impelled forwards by the multitude, without any counteracting influence?</hi> Seneca, <hi type="italic">Epist.</hi> 29. This discourages many: they are loth to be singular, to be solitary; but instead of stumbling at this, say rather, If so few are going to heaven, there shall be one the more for me. <div eID="gen21730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21731" type="x-p"/> [2.] Let us see what there is in this way, which, notwithstanding this, should invite us all to it; it <hi type="italic">leads to life,</hi> to present comfort in the favour of God, which is the life of the soul; to eternal bliss, the hope of which, at the end of our way, should reconcile us to all the difficulties and inconveniences of the road. Life and godliness are put together (<reference osisRef="2Pet.1.3">2 Pet. i. 3</reference>); <hi type="italic">The gate is strait and the way narrow</hi> and up-hill, but one hour in heaven will make amends for it. <div eID="gen21731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21732" type="x-p"/> 2. The great concern and duty of every one of us, in consideration of all this; <hi type="italic">Enter ye in at the strait gate.</hi> The matter is fairly stated; life and death, good and evil, are set before us; both the ways, and both the ends: now let the matter be taken entire, and considered impartially, and then choose you this day which you will walk in; nay, the matter determines itself, and will not admit of a debate. No man, in his wits, would choose to go to the gallows, because it is a smooth, pleasant way to it, nor refuse the offer of a palace and a throne, because it is a rough, dirty way to it; yet such absurdities as these are men guilty of, in the concerns of their souls. Delay not, therefore; deliberate not any longer, but <hi type="italic">enter ye in at the strait gate;</hi> <hi type="italic">knock</hi> at it by sincere and constant prayers and endeavors, <hi type="italic">and it shall be opened;</hi> nay, a wide door shall be opened, and an effectual one. It is true, we can neither go in, nor go on, without the assistance of divine grace; but it is as true, that grace is freely offered, and shall not be wanting to those that seek it, and submit to it. Conversion is hard work, but it is needful, and, blessed be God, it is not impossible if we strive, <reference osisRef="Luke.13.24">Luke xiii. 24</reference>.
entries.635c2d34733914c7c36411ea7170be9296eb22ce: <div eID="gen21732" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Sermon on the Mount.</title> <div sID="gen21733" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves. <hi type="super">16</hi> Ye shall know them by their fruits. Do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles? <hi type="super">17</hi> Even so every good tree bringeth forth good fruit; but a corrupt tree bringeth forth evil fruit. <hi type="super">18</hi> A good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit, neither <hi type="italic">can</hi> a corrupt tree bring forth good fruit. <hi type="super">19</hi> Every tree that bringeth not forth good fruit is hewn down, and cast into the fire. <hi type="super">20</hi> Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them. <div eID="gen21733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21734" type="x-p"/> We have here a caution against <hi type="italic">false prophets,</hi> to take heed that we be not deceived and imposed upon by them. <hi type="italic">Prophets</hi> are properly such as foretel things to come; there are some mentioned in the Old Testament, who pretended to that without warrant, and the event disproved their pretensions, as Zedekiah, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.11">1 Kings xxii. 11</reference>, and another Zedekiah, <reference osisRef="Jer.29.21">Jer. xxix. 21</reference>. But <hi type="italic">prophets</hi> did also teach the people their duty, so that <hi type="italic">false prophets</hi> here are false teachers. Christ being a Prophet and <hi type="italic">a Teacher come from God,</hi> and designing to send abroad teachers under him, gives warning to all to take heed of counterfeits, who, instead of healing souls with wholesome doctrine, as they pretend, would poison them. <div eID="gen21734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21735" type="x-p"/> They are false teachers and <hi type="italic">false prophets,</hi> 1. Who produce false commissions, who pretend to have immediate warrant and direction from God to set up for <hi type="italic">prophets,</hi> and to be divinely inspired, when they are not so. Though their doctrine may be true, we are to <hi type="italic">beware</hi> of them as <hi type="italic">false prophets.</hi> False apostles are those who <hi type="italic">say they are apostles, and are not</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.2.2">Rev. ii. 2</reference>); such are <hi type="italic">false prophets.</hi> "Take heed of those who pretend to revelation, and admit them not without sufficient proof, lest that one absurdity being admitted, a thousand follow." 2. Who preach false doctrine in those things that are essential to religion; who teach that which is contrary to <hi type="italic">the truth as it is in Jesus,</hi> to <hi type="italic">the truth which is accordingly to godliness.</hi> The former seems to be the proper notion of <hi type="italic">pseudo-propheta,</hi> a <hi type="italic">false</hi> or pretending <hi type="italic">prophet,</hi> but commonly the latter falls in with it; for who would hang out false colours, but with design, under pretence of them, the more successfully to attack the truth. "Well, beware of them, suspect them, try them, and when you have discovered their falsehood, avoid them, have nothing to do with them. Stand upon your guard against this temptation, which commonly attends the days of reformation, and the breakings out of divine light in more than ordinary strength and splendour." When God's work is revived, Satan and his agents are most busy. Here is, <div eID="gen21735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21736" type="x-p"/> I. A good reason for this caution, <hi type="italic">Beware of</hi> them, for they are <hi type="italic">wolves in sheep's clothing,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.7.15">v. 15</reference>. <div eID="gen21736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21737" type="x-p"/> 1. We have need to be very cautious, because their pretences are very fair and plausible, and such as will deceive us, if we be not upon our guard. They <hi type="italic">come in sheep's clothing,</hi> in the habit of <hi type="italic">prophets,</hi> which was plain and coarse, and unwrought; they <hi type="italic">wear a rough garment to deceive,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.13.4">Zech. xiii. 4</reference>. Elijah's mantle the Septuagint calls <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">he melote</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">a sheep-skin</hi> mantle. We must take heed of being imposed upon by men's dress and garb, as by that of the scribes, who <hi type="italic">desire to walk in long robes,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.20.46">Luke xx. 46</reference>. Or it may be taken figuratively; they pretend to be sheep, and outwardly appear so innocent, harmless, meek, useful, and all that is good, as to be excelled by none; they feign themselves to be just men, and for the sake of their clothing are admitted among the sheep, which gives them an opportunity of doing them a mischief ere they are aware. They and their errors are gilded with the specious pretences of sanctity and devotion. Satan turns himself <hi type="italic">into an angel of light,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.13-2Cor.11.14">2 Cor. xi. 13, 14</reference>. The enemy has <hi type="italic">horns like a lamb</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.13.11">Rev. xiii. 11</reference>); <hi type="italic">faces of men,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.9.7-Rev.9.8">Rev. ix. 7, 8</reference>. Seducers in language and carriage are <hi type="italic">soft as wool,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.16.18">Rom. xvi. 18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.30.10">Isa. xxx. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen21737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21738" type="x-p"/> 2. Because under these pretensions their designs are very malicious and mischievous; <hi type="italic">inwardly they are ravening wolves.</hi> Every <hi type="italic">hypocrite</hi> is a <hi type="italic">goat</hi> in sheep's clothing; not only not a sheep, but the worst enemy the sheep has, that comes not but to tear and devour, to <hi type="italic">scatter the sheep</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.10.12">John x. 12</reference>), to drive them from God, and from one another, into crooked paths. Those that would cheat us of any truth, and possess us with error, whatever they pretend, design mischief to our souls. Paul calls them <hi type="italic">grievous wolves,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.20.29">Acts xx. 29</reference>. They raven for themselves, <hi type="italic">serve their own belly</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.16.18">Rom. xvi. 18</reference>), make a prey of you, make a gain of you. Now since it is so easy a thing, and withal so dangerous, to be cheated, <hi type="italic">Beware of false prophets.</hi> <div eID="gen21738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21739" type="x-p"/> II. Here is a good rule to go by in this caution; we must <hi type="italic">prove all things</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.21">1 Thess. v. 21</reference>), <hi type="italic">try the spirits</hi> (<reference osisRef="1John.4.1">1 John iv. 1</reference>), and here we have a touchstone; <hi type="italic">ye shall know them by their fruits,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.7.16-Matt.7.20">v. 16-20</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen21739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21740" type="x-p"/> 1. The illustration of this comparison, of the fruit's being the discovery of the tree. You cannot always distinguish them by their bark and leaves, nor by the spreading of their boughs, but <hi type="italic">by their fruits ye shall know them.</hi> The fruit is according to the tree. Men may, in their professions, put a force upon their nature, and contradict their inward principles, but the stream and bent of their practices will agree with them. Christ insists upon this, the agreeableness between the fruit and the tree, which is such as that, (1.) If you know what the tree is, you may know what fruit to expect. Never look to gather <hi type="italic">grapes from thorns, nor figs from thistles;</hi> it is not in their nature to produce such fruits. An apple may be stuck, or a bunch of grapes may hang, upon a thorn; so may a good truth, a good word or action, be found in a bad man, but you may be sure it never grew there. Note, [1.] Corrupt, vicious, unsanctified hearts are like thorns and thistles, which came in with sin, are worthless, vexing, and for the fire at last. [2.] Good works are <hi type="italic">good fruit,</hi> like grapes and figs, pleasing to God and profitable to men. [3.] This <hi type="italic">good fruit</hi> is never to be expected from bad men, and more than <hi type="italic">a clean thing out of an unclean:</hi> they want an influencing acceptable principle. <hi type="italic">Out of</hi> an <hi type="italic">evil treasure</hi> will be brought forth <hi type="italic">evil things.</hi> (2.) On the other hand, if you know what the fruit is, you may, by that, perceive what the tree is. <hi type="italic">A good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit;</hi> and <hi type="italic">a corrupt tree cannot bring forth good fruit,</hi> nay, it cannot but <hi type="italic">bring forth evil fruit.</hi> But then that must be reckoned the fruit of the tree which it brings forth naturally and which is its genuine product—which it brings forth plentifully and constantly and which is its usual product. Men are known, not by particular acts, but by the course and tenour of their conversation, and by the more frequent acts, especially those that appear to be free, and most their own, and least under the influence of external motives and inducements. <div eID="gen21740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21741" type="x-p"/> 2. The application of this to the false prophets. <div eID="gen21741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21742" type="x-p"/> (1.) By way of terror and threatening (<reference osisRef="Matt.7.19">v. 19</reference>); <hi type="italic">Every tree that brings not forth good fruit is hewn down.</hi> This very saying John the Baptist had used, <reference osisRef="Matt.3.10">ch. iii. 10</reference>. Christ could have spoken the same sense in other words; could have altered it, or given it a new turn; but he thought it no disparagement to him to say the same that John had said before him; let not ministers be ambitious of coining new expressions, nor people's ears itch for novelties; to write and speak the same things must not be grievous, for it is safe. Here is, [1.] The description of barren trees; they are trees that do <hi type="italic">not bring forth good fruit;</hi> though there be fruit, if it be not <hi type="italic">good fruit</hi> (though that be done, which for the matter of it is good, if it be not done well, in a right manner, and for a right end), the tree is accounted barren. [2.] The doom of barren trees; <hi type="italic">they are,</hi> that is, certainly they shall be, <hi type="italic">hewn down, and cast into the fire;</hi> God will deal with them as men use to deal with dry trees that cumber the ground: he will mark them by some signal tokens of his displeasure, he will bark them by stripping them of their parts and gifts, and will cut them <hi type="italic">down</hi> by death, <hi type="italic">and cast</hi> them <hi type="italic">into the fire</hi> of hell, a fire blown with the bellows of God's wrath, and fed with the wood of barren trees. Compare this with <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.12-Ezek.31.13">Ezek. xxxi. 12, 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.4.14">Dan. iv. 14</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.15.6">John xv. 6</reference>. <div eID="gen21742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21743" type="x-p"/> (2.) By way of trial; <hi type="italic">By their fruits ye shall know them.</hi> <div eID="gen21743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21744" type="x-p"/> [1.] <hi type="italic">By the fruits</hi> of their persons, their words and actions, and the course of their conversation. If you would know whether they be right or not, observe how they live; their works will testify for them or against them. The scribes and Pharisees sat in Moses's chair, and taught the law, but they were proud, and covetous, and false, and oppressive, and therefore Christ warned him disciples to <hi type="italic">beware of</hi> them and of their <hi type="italic">leaven,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.12.38">Mark xii. 38</reference>. If men pretend to be prophets and are immoral, that disproves their pretensions; those are no true friends <hi type="italic">to the cross of Christ,</hi> whatever they profess, <hi type="italic">whose God is their belly,</hi> and <hi type="italic">whose mind earthly things,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.3.18-Phil.3.19">Phil. iii. 18, 19</reference>. Those are not taught nor sent of the holy God, whose lives evidence that they are led by the unclean spirit. God puts the treasure into earthen vessels, but not into such corrupt vessels: they may declare God's statutes, but what have they to do to declare them? <div eID="gen21744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21745" type="x-p"/> [2.] <hi type="italic">By the fruits</hi> of their doctrine; their fruits as prophets: not that this is the only way, but it is one way, of trying doctrines, <hi type="italic">whether they be of God</hi> or not. What do they tend to do? What affections and practices will they lead those into, that embrace them? If <hi type="italic">the doctrine be of God,</hi> it will tend to promote serious piety, humility, charity, holiness, and love, with other Christian graces; but if, on the contrary, the doctrines these prophets preach have a manifest tendency to make people proud, worldly, and contentious, to make them loose and careless in their conversations, unjust or uncharitable, factious or disturbers of the public peace; if it indulge carnal liberty, and take people off from governing themselves and their families by the strict rules of <hi type="italic">the narrow way,</hi> we may conclude, that <hi type="italic">this persuasion comes not of him that calleth us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.5.8">Gal. v. 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">This wisdom is from above,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.3.15">James iii. 15</reference>. <hi type="italic">Faith and a good conscience</hi> are held together, <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.19">1 Tim. i. 19</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.9">iii. 9</reference>. Note, <hi type="italic">Doctrines of doubtful disputation</hi> must be tried by graces and duties of confessed certainty: those opinions come not from God that lead to sin: but if we cannot <hi type="italic">know them by their fruits,</hi> we must have recourse to the great touchstone, to the law, and to the testimony; do they speak according to that rule?
entries.0e48c5616b46563fca083c205296fcf4c15bfd88: <div eID="gen21745" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Sermon on the Mount.</title> <div sID="gen21746" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven. <hi type="super">22</hi> Many will say to me in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name? and in thy name have cast out devils? and in thy name done many wonderful works? <hi type="super">23</hi> And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity. <hi type="super">24</hi> Therefore whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock: 25 And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell not: for it was founded upon a rock. <hi type="super">26</hi> And every one that heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them not, shall be likened unto a foolish man, which built his house upon the sand: <hi type="super">27</hi> And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell: and great was the fall of it. <hi type="super">28</hi> And it came to pass, when Jesus had ended these sayings, the people were astonished at his doctrine: <hi type="super">29</hi> For he taught them as <hi type="italic">one</hi> having authority, and not as the scribes. <div eID="gen21746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21747" type="x-p"/> We have here the conclusion of this long and excellent sermon, the scope of which is to show the indispensable necessity of obedience to the commands of Christ; this is designed to clench the nail, that it might fix in a sure place: he speaks this to his disciples, that sat at his feet whenever he preached, and followed him wherever he went. Had he sought his own praise among men, he would have said, that was enough; but the religion he came to establish is in power, not in word only (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.20">1 Cor. iv. 20</reference>), and therefore something more is necessary. <div eID="gen21747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21748" type="x-p"/> I. He shows, by a plain remonstrance, that an outward profession of religion, however remarkable, will not bring us to heaven, unless there be a correspondent conversation, <reference osisRef="Matt.7.21-Matt.7.23">v. 21-23</reference>. All judgment is committed to our Lord Jesus; the keys are put into his hand; he has power to prescribe new terms of life and death, and to judge men according to them: now this is a solemn declaration pursuant to that power. Observe here, <div eID="gen21748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21749" type="x-p"/> 1. Christ's law laid down, <reference osisRef="Matt.7.21">v. 21</reference>. <hi type="italic">Not every one that saith, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven, into the kingdom of</hi> grace and glory. It is an answer to that question, <reference osisRef="Ps.15.1">Ps. xv. 1</reference>. <hi type="italic">Who shall sojourn in thy tabernacle?</hi>—the church militant; <hi type="italic">and who shall dwell in thy holy hill?</hi>—the church triumphant. Christ here shows, <div eID="gen21749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21750" type="x-p"/> (1.) That it will not suffice to say, <hi type="italic">Lord, Lord;</hi> in word and tongue to own Christ for our Master, and to make addresses to him, and professions of him accordingly: in prayer to God, in discourse with men, we must call Christ, <hi type="italic">Lord, Lord;</hi> we <hi type="italic">say well,</hi> for <hi type="italic">so he is</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.13.13">John xiii. 13</reference>); but can we imagine that this is enough to bring us to heaven, that such a piece of formality as this should be so recompensed, or that he who knows and requires the heart should be so put off with shows for substance? Compliments among men are pieces of civility that are returned with compliments, but they are never paid as real services; and can they then be of an account with Christ? There may be a seeming importunity in prayer, <hi type="italic">Lord, Lord:</hi> but if inward <hi type="italic">im</hi>pressions be not answerable to outward <hi type="italic">ex</hi>pressions, we are but <hi type="italic">as sounding brass and a tinkling cymbal.</hi> This is not to take us off from saying, <hi type="italic">Lord, Lord;</hi> from praying, and being earnest in prayer, from professing Christ's name, and being bold in professing it, but from resting in these, in the <hi type="italic">form of godliness,</hi> without <hi type="italic">the power.</hi> <div eID="gen21750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21751" type="x-p"/> (2.) That it is necessary to our happiness that we <hi type="italic">do the will of</hi> Christ, which is indeed <hi type="italic">the will of</hi> his <hi type="italic">Father in heaven.</hi> <hi type="italic">The will of</hi> God, as Christ's <hi type="italic">Father,</hi> is his will in the gospel, for there he is made known, as <hi type="italic">the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ:</hi> and in him our Father. Now this is his will, that we believe in Christ, that we repent of sin, that we live a holy life, that we <hi type="italic">love one another. This is his will, even our sanctification.</hi> If we comply not with the will of God, we mock Christ in calling him <hi type="italic">Lord,</hi> as those did who put on him a gorgeous robe, and said, <hi type="italic">Hail, King of the Jews.</hi> Saying and doing are two things, often parted in conversation of men: he that said, <hi type="italic">I go, sir,</hi> stirred never a step (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.30">ch. xxi. 30</reference>); but these two things <hi type="italic">God has joined</hi> in his command, and <hi type="italic">let no man</hi> that <hi type="italic">puts</hi> them <hi type="italic">asunder</hi> think to <hi type="italic">enter into the kingdom of heaven.</hi> <div eID="gen21751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21752" type="x-p"/> 2. The hypocrite's plea against the strictness of this law, offering other things in lieu of obedience, <reference osisRef="Matt.7.22">v. 22</reference>. The plea is supposed to be <hi type="italic">in that day,</hi> that great day, when every man shall appear in his own colours; <hi type="italic">when the secrets of all hearts shall be</hi> manifest, and among the rest, the secret pretences with which sinners now support their vain hopes. Christ knows the strength of their cause, and it is but weakness; what they now harbour in their bosoms, they will then produce in arrest of judgment to stay the doom, but it will be in vain. They put in their plea with great importunity, <hi type="italic">Lord, Lord;</hi> and with great confidence, appealing to Christ concerning it; <hi type="italic">Lord,</hi> does thou not know, (1.) That <hi type="italic">we have prophesied in thy name?</hi> Yes, it may be so; Balaam and Caiaphas were overruled to prophesy, and Saul was against his will <hi type="italic">among the prophets,</hi> yet that did not save them. These <hi type="italic">prophesied in</hi> his <hi type="italic">name,</hi> but he did not send them; they only made use of his name to serve a turn. Note, A man may be a preacher, may have gifts for the ministry, and an external call to it, and perhaps some success in it, and yet be a wicked man; may help others to heaven, and yet come short himself. (2.) That <hi type="italic">in thy name we have cast out devils?</hi> That may be too; Judas <hi type="italic">cast out devils,</hi> and yet was a <hi type="italic">son of perdition.</hi> Origen says, that in his time so prevalent was the name of Christ to <hi type="italic">cast out devils,</hi> that sometimes it availed when named by wicked Christians. A man might <hi type="italic">cast devils out</hi> of others, and yet have a devil, nay, be a devil himself. (3.) That <hi type="italic">in thy name we have done many wonderful works.</hi> There may be a faith of miracles, where there is no justifying faith; none of that <hi type="italic">faith which works by love</hi> and obedience. Gifts of tongues and healing would recommend men to the world, but it is real holiness or sanctification that is accepted of God. Grace and love are <hi type="italic">a more excellent way</hi> than <hi type="italic">removing mountains,</hi> or <hi type="italic">speaking with the tongues of men and of angels,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.13.1-1Cor.13.2">1 Cor. xiii. 1, 2</reference>. Grace will bring a man to heaven without working miracles, but working miracles will never bring a man to heaven without grace. Observe, That which their heart was upon, in doing these works, and which they confided in, was the wonderfulness of them. Simon Magus wondered at the miracles (<reference osisRef="Acts.8.13">Acts viii. 13</reference>), and therefore would give any money for power to do the like. Observe, They had not many good works to plead: they could not pretend to have done many gracious works of piety and charity; one such would have passed better in their account than <hi type="italic">many wonderful works,</hi> which availed not at all, while they persisted in disobedience. Miracles have now ceased, and with them this plea; but do not carnal hearts still encourage themselves in their groundless hopes, with the like vain supports? They think they shall go to heaven, because they have been of good repute among professors of religion, have kept fasts, and given alms, and have been preferred in the church; as if this would atone for their reigning pride, worldliness, and sensuality; and want of love to God and man. <hi type="italic">Bethel is their confidence</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.48.13">Jer. xlviii. 13</reference>), they are <hi type="italic">haughty because of the holy mountain</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zeph.3.11">Zeph. iii. 11</reference>); and boast that they are <hi type="italic">the temple of the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.7.4">Jer. vii. 4</reference>. Let us take heed of resting in external privileges and performances, lest <hi type="italic">we deceive ourselves,</hi> and perish eternally, as multitudes do, <hi type="italic">with a lie in our right hand.</hi> <div eID="gen21752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21753" type="x-p"/> 3. The rejection of this plea as frivolous. The same that is the Law-Maker (<reference osisRef="Matt.7.21">v. 21</reference>) is here the Judge according to that law (<reference osisRef="Matt.7.23">v. 23</reference>), and he will overrule the plea, will overrule it publicly; he <hi type="italic">will profess to them</hi> with all possible solemnity, as sentence is passed by the Judge, <hi type="italic">I never knew you,</hi> and therefore <hi type="italic">depart from me, ye that work iniquity.</hi>—Observe, (1.) Why, and upon what ground, he rejects them and their plea—because they were <hi type="italic">workers for iniquity.</hi> Note, It is possible for men to have a great name for piety, and yet to be <hi type="italic">workers of iniquity;</hi> and those that are so will <hi type="italic">receive the greater damnation.</hi> Secret haunts of sin, kept under the cloak of a visible profession, will be the ruin of the hypocrites. Living in known sin nullifies men's pretensions, be they ever so specious. (2.) How it is expressed; <hi type="italic">I never knew you;</hi> "I never owned you as my servants, no, not when you <hi type="italic">prophesied in</hi> my <hi type="italic">name,</hi> when you were in the height of your profession, and were most extolled." This intimates, that if he had ever known them, as <hi type="italic">the Lord knows them that are his,</hi> had ever owned them and loved them as his, he would have known them, and owned them, and <hi type="italic">loved them, to the end;</hi> but he <hi type="italic">never</hi> did <hi type="italic">know</hi> them, for he always knew them to be hypocrites, and rotten at heart, as he did Judas; therefore, says he, <hi type="italic">depart from me.</hi> Has Christ need of such guests? When he came in the flesh, he called sinners <hi type="italic">to</hi> him (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.13">ch. ix. 13</reference>), but <hi type="italic">when he shall come again in glory,</hi> he will drive sinners <hi type="italic">from</hi> him. They that would not <hi type="italic">come to</hi> him to be saved, must <hi type="italic">depart from</hi> him to be damned. To <hi type="italic">depart from</hi> Christ is the very hell of hell; it is the foundation of all the misery of the damned, to be cut off from all hope of benefit from Christ and he mediation. Those that go no further in Christ's service than a bare profession, he does not accept, nor will he own them in the great day. See from what a height of hope men may fall into the depth of misery! How they may go to hell, by the gates of heaven! This should be an awakening word to all Christians. If a preacher, one that <hi type="italic">cast out devils,</hi> and wrought miracles, be disowned of Christ for <hi type="italic">working iniquity;</hi> what will become of us, if we be found such? And if we <hi type="italic">be</hi> such, we shall certainly be found such. At God's bar, a profession of religion will not bear out any man in the practice and indulgence of sin; therefore <hi type="italic">let every one that names the name of Christ, depart from all iniquity.</hi> <div eID="gen21753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21754" type="x-p"/> II. He shows, by a parable, that hearing these sayings of Christ will not make us happy, if we do not make conscience of doing them; but that if we hear them and do them, we are <hi type="italic">blessed in our deed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.7.24-Matt.7.27">v. 24-27</reference>. <div eID="gen21754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21755" type="x-p"/> 1. The hearers of Christ's word are here divided into two sorts; some that hear, and do what they hear; others that hear and do not.
