Christ preached now to a mixed multitude, and he thus <hi type="italic">separates them, one from the other,</hi> as he will at the great day, when <hi type="italic">all nations shall be gathered before him.</hi> Christ is still speaking from heaven by his word and Spirits, speaks by ministers, by providences, and of those that hear him there are two sorts. <div eID="gen21755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21756" type="x-p"/> (1.) Some that <hi type="italic">hear his sayings and do them:</hi> blessed be God that there are any such, though comparatively few. To hear Christ is not barely to give him the hearing, but to obey him. Note, It highly concerns us all to do what we <hi type="italic">hear</hi> of the saying of Christ. It is a mercy that we <hi type="italic">hear</hi> his <hi type="italic">sayings: Blessed are those ears,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.13.16-Matt.13.17">ch. xiii. 16, 17</reference>. But, if we practise not what we hear, we <hi type="italic">receive</hi> that <hi type="italic">grace in vain.</hi> To <hi type="italic">do</hi> Christ's <hi type="italic">sayings</hi> is conscientiously to abstain from the sins that he forbids, and to perform the duties that he requires. Our thoughts and affections, our words and actions, the temper of our minds, and the tenour of our lives, must be conformable to the gospel of Christ; that is the doing he requires. All the <hi type="italic">sayings</hi> of Christ, not only the laws he has enacted, but the truths he has revealed, must be done by us. <hi type="italic">They are a light,</hi> not only to <hi type="italic">our eyes,</hi> but <hi type="italic">to our feet,</hi> and are designed not only to <hi type="italic">in</hi>form our judgments, but to <hi type="italic">re</hi>form our hearts and lives: nor do we indeed believe them, if we do not live up to them. Observe, It is not enough to <hi type="italic">hear</hi> Christ's <hi type="italic">sayings,</hi> and understand them, <hi type="italic">hear</hi> them, and remember them, <hi type="italic">hear</hi> them, and talk of them, repeat them, dispute for them; but we must <hi type="italic">hear, and do</hi> them. <hi type="italic">This do, and thou shalt live.</hi> Those only <hi type="italic">that hear, and do,</hi> are <hi type="italic">blessed</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.11.28">Luke xi. 28</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.13.17">John xiii. 17</reference>), and are akin to Christ. <reference osisRef="Matt.12.50">ch. xii. 50</reference>. <div eID="gen21756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21757" type="x-p"/> (2.) There are others who <hi type="italic">hear</hi> Christ's <hi type="italic">sayings and do them not;</hi> their religion rests in bare hearing, and goes no further; like children that have the rickets, their heads swell with empty notions, and indigested opinions, but their joints are weak, and they heavy and listless; they neither can stir, nor care to stir, in any good duty; <hi type="italic">they hear</hi> God's <hi type="italic">words,</hi> as if they desired to <hi type="italic">know his ways,</hi> like a people <hi type="italic">that did righteousness, but they will not do them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.33.30-Ezek.33.31">Ezek. xxxiii. 30, 31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.58.2">Isa. lviii. 2</reference>. Thus they deceive themselves, as Micah, who thought himself happy, because he had a Levite to be his priest, though he had not the Lord to be his God. The seed is sown, but it never comes up; they see their spots in the glass of the word, but wash them off, <reference osisRef="Jas.1.22">Jam. i. 22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jas.1.24">24</reference>. Thus they put a cheat upon their own souls; for it is certain, if our hearing be not the means of our obedience, it will be the aggravation of our disobedience. Those who only <hi type="italic">hear</hi> Christ's <hi type="italic">sayings, and do them not,</hi> sit down in the midway to heaven, and that will never bring them to their journey's end. They are akin to Christ only by the half-blood, and our law allows not such to inherit. <div eID="gen21757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21758" type="x-p"/> 2. These two sorts of hearers are here represented in their true characters, and the state of their case, under the comparison of two builders; one was <hi type="italic">wise,</hi> and <hi type="italic">built upon a rock,</hi> and his building stood in a storm; the other <hi type="italic">foolish,</hi> and <hi type="italic">built upon the sand,</hi> and his building fell. <div eID="gen21758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21759" type="x-p"/> Now, (1.) The general scope of this parable teaches us that the only way to make sure work for our souls and eternity is, to <hi type="italic">hear and do the sayings of</hi> the Lord Jesus, <hi type="italic">these sayings of</hi> his in this sermon upon the mount, which is wholly practical; some of them seem hard sayings to flesh and blood, but they must be done; and thus we <hi type="italic">lay up in store a good foundation for the time to come</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.19">1 Tim. vi. 19</reference>); a <hi type="italic">good bond,</hi> so some read it; a bond of God's making, which secures salvation upon gospel-terms, that is <hi type="italic">a good bond;</hi> not one of our own devising, which brings salvation to our own fancies. They make sure the <hi type="italic">good part,</hi> who, like Mary, when they hear the word of Christ, <hi type="italic">sit at his feet</hi> in subjection to it: <hi type="italic">Speak, Lord, for thy servant heareth.</hi> <div eID="gen21759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21760" type="x-p"/> (2.) The particular parts of it teach us divers good lessons. <div eID="gen21760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21761" type="x-p"/> [1.] That we have every one of us a house to build, and that house is our hope for heaven. It ought to be our chief and constant care, to <hi type="italic">make our calling and election sure,</hi> and so we make our salvation sure; to secure a title to heaven's happiness, and then to get the comfortable evidence of it; to make it sure, and sure to ourselves, <hi type="italic">that when we fail, we</hi> shall <hi type="italic">be received into everlasting habitations.</hi> Many never mind this: it is the furthest thing from their thoughts; they are building for this world, as if they were to be here always, but take no care to build for another world. All who take upon them a profession of religion, profess to enquire, what they shall <hi type="italic">do to be saved;</hi> how they may get to heaven at last, and may have a well-grounded hope of it in the mean time. <div eID="gen21761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21762" type="x-p"/> [2.] That there is <hi type="italic">a rock</hi> provided for us to build this house upon, <hi type="italic">and that rock is Christ.</hi> He is <hi type="italic">laid for a foundation,</hi> and <hi type="italic">other foundation can no man lay,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.28.16">Isa. xxviii. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.11">1 Cor. iii. 11</reference>. He <hi type="italic">is our Hope,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.1">1 Tim. i. 1</reference>. Christ in us is so; we must ground our hopes of heaven upon the fulness of Christ's merit, for the pardon of sin, the power of his Spirit, for the sanctification of our nature, and the prevalency of his intercession, for the conveyance of all that good which he has purchased for us. There is that in him, as <hi type="italic">he is made known,</hi> and made over, <hi type="italic">to us in the gospel,</hi> which is sufficient to redress all our grievances, and to answer all the necessities of our case, so that he is <hi type="italic">a Saviour to the uttermost.</hi> The church is <hi type="italic">built upon this Rock,</hi> and so is every believer. He is strong and immovable as a <hi type="italic">rock;</hi> we may venture our all upon him, and shall not be made <hi type="italic">ashamed of our hope.</hi> <div eID="gen21762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21763" type="x-p"/> [3.] That there is a remnant, who by hearing and doing the <hi type="italic">sayings of</hi> Christ, build their hopes <hi type="italic">upon this Rock;</hi> and it is their wisdom. Christ is our only <hi type="italic">Way to the Father,</hi> and the obedience of faith is our only <hi type="italic">way</hi> to Christ: for <hi type="italic">to them that obey him,</hi> and to <hi type="italic">them</hi> only, he <hi type="italic">becomes the Author of eternal salvation.</hi> Those <hi type="italic">build upon</hi> Christ, who having sincerely consented to him, as their Prince and Saviour, make it their constant care to conform to all the rules of his holy religion, and therein depend entirely upon him for assistance from God, and acceptance with him, <hi type="italic">and count</hi> every <hi type="italic">thing but loss and dung that they may win Christ,</hi> and be found in him. Building <hi type="italic">upon a rock</hi> requires care and pains: they that would make their <hi type="italic">calling and election sure,</hi> must <hi type="italic">give diligence.</hi> They are wise builders who <hi type="italic">begin to build</hi> so as they may be <hi type="italic">able to finish</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.14.30">Luke xiv. 30</reference>), and therefore lay a firm foundation. <div eID="gen21763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21764" type="x-p"/> [4.] That there are many who profess that they hope to go to heaven, but despise this <hi type="italic">Rock,</hi> and build their hopes <hi type="italic">upon the sand;</hi> which is done without much pains, but it is their folly. Every thing besides Christ is sand. Some build their hopes upon their worldly prosperity, as if they were a sure token of God's favour, <reference osisRef="Hos.12.8">Hos. xii. 8</reference>. Others upon their external profession of religion, the privileges they enjoy, and the performances they go through in that profession, and the reputation they have got by it. They are called Christians, were baptized, go to church, hear Christ's word, say their prayers, and do nobody any harm, and, if they perish, God help a great many! This is the light of their own fire, which they walk in; this is that, upon which, with a great deal of assurance, they venture; but it is all sand, too weak to bear such a fabric as our hopes of heaven. <div eID="gen21764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21765" type="x-p"/> [5.] That there is a storm coming, that will try what our hopes are bottomed on; <hi type="italic">will try every man's work</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.13">1 Cor. iii. 13</reference>); <hi type="italic">will discover the foundation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hab.3.13">Hab. iii. 13</reference>. <hi type="italic">Rain, and floods, and wind, will beat upon the house;</hi> the trial is sometimes in this world; <hi type="italic">when tribulation and persecution arise because of the word,</hi> then it will be seen, who only heard the word, and who heard and practiced it; then when we have occasion to use our hopes, it will be tried whether they were right, and well-grounded, or not. However, when death and judgment come, then the storm comes, and it will undoubtedly come, how calm soever things may be with us now. Then every thing else will fail us but these hopes, and then, if ever, they will be turned into everlasting fruition. <div eID="gen21765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21766" type="x-p"/> [6.] That those hopes which are built upon Christ the Rock will stand, and will stand the builder in stead when the storm comes; they will be his preservation, both from desertion, and from prevailing disquiet. His profession will not wither; his comforts will not fail; they will be his strength and song, <hi type="italic">as an anchor of the soul, sure and steadfast.</hi> When he comes to the last encounter, those hopes will take off the terror of death and the grave; will carry him cheerfully through that dark valley; will be approved by the Judge; will stand the test of the great day; and will be crowned with endless glory, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.12">2 Cor. i. 12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.7-2Tim.4.8">2 Tim. iv. 7, 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">Blessed is that servant, whom his Lord, when he comes, finds so doing,</hi> so hoping. <div eID="gen21766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21767" type="x-p"/> [7.] That those hopes which foolish builders ground upon any thing but Christ, will certainly fail them on a stormy day; will yield them no true comfort and satisfaction in trouble, in the hour of death, and in the day of judgment; will be no fence against temptations to apostacy, in a time of persecution. <hi type="italic">When God takes away the soul, where is the hope of the hypocrite?</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.27.8">Job xxvii. 8</reference>. It is as <hi type="italic">the spider's web,</hi> and as <hi type="italic">the giving up of the ghost.</hi> He shall <hi type="italic">lean upon his house, but it shall not stand,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.8.14-Job.8.15">Job viii. 14, 15</reference>. It fell in the storm, when the builder had most need of it, and expected it would be a shelter to him. It fell when it was too late to build another: <hi type="italic">when a wicked man dies, his expectation perishes;</hi> then, when he thought it would have been turned into fruition, <hi type="italic">it fell, and great was the fall of it.</hi> It was a great disappointment to the builder; the shame and loss were great. The higher men's hopes have been raised, the lower they fall. It is the sorest ruin of all that attends formal professors; witness Capernaum's doom. <div eID="gen21767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21768" type="x-p"/> III. In the <reference osisRef="Matt.7.28-Matt.7.29">two last verses</reference>, we are told what impressions Christ's discourse made upon the auditory. It was an excellent sermon; and it is probable that he said more than is here recorded; and doubtless the delivery of it from the mouth of him, into whose lips grace was poured, did mightily set if off. Now, 1. <hi type="italic">They were astonished at this doctrine;</hi> it is to be feared that few of them were brought by it to follow him: but for the present, they were filled with wonder. Note, It is possible for people to admire good preaching, and yet to remain in ignorance and unbelief; to be astonished, and yet not sanctified. 2. The reason was because he taught them <hi type="italic">as one having authority, and not as the scribes.</hi> The scribes pretended to as much authority as any teachers whatsoever, and were supported by all the external advantages that could be obtained, but their preaching was mean, and flat, and jejune: they spake as those what were not themselves masters of what they preached: the word did not come from them with any life or force; they delivered it as a school-boy says his lesson; but Christ delivered his discourse, as a judge gives his charge. He did indeed, <hi type="italic">dominari in conscionibus—deliver his discourses with a tone of authority;</hi> his lessons were law; his word a word of command. Christ, upon the mountain, showed more true authority, than the scribes in Moses's seat. Thus when Christ teaches by his Spirit in the soul, he teaches with authority. He says, <hi type="italic">Let there be light, and there is light.</hi>  <chapter eID="Matt.7"/> <div eID="gen21768" type="x-p"/>

entries.8d068d4cf7552eb2f4b2f71c27ed4dc736b4ea23: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13433"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 7</title> <div sID="gen25625" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Sermon on the Mount--</hi>concluded.<div eID="gen25625" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.7.1-Matt.7.12">Mt 7:1-12</reference>. Miscellaneous Supplementary Counsels.</title> <div sID="gen25626" type="x-p"/> That these verses are entirely supplementary is the simplest and most natural view of them. All attempts to make out any evident connection with the immediately preceding context are, in our judgment, forced. But, though supplementary, these counsels are far from being of subordinate importance. On the contrary, they involve some of the most delicate and vital duties of the Christian life. In the vivid form in which they are here presented, perhaps they could not have been introduced with the same effect under any of the foregoing heads; but they spring out of the same great principles, and are but other forms and manifestations of the same evangelical "righteousness."<div eID="gen25626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25627" type="x-p"/> Censorious Judgment (<reference osisRef="Matt.7.1-Matt.7.5">Mt 7:1-5</reference>).<div eID="gen25627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25628" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13433"/><hi type="bold">1. Judge not, that ye be not judged--</hi>To "judge" here does not exactly mean to pronounce condemnatory judgment, nor does it refer to simple judging at all, whether favorable or the reverse. The context makes it clear that the thing here condemned is that disposition to look unfavorably on the character and actions of others, which leads invariably to the pronouncing of rash, unjust, and unlovely judgments upon them. No doubt it is the judgments so pronounced which are here spoken of; but what our Lord aims at is the spirit out of which they spring. Provided we eschew this unlovely spirit, we are not only warranted to sit in judgment upon a brother's character and actions, but in the exercise of a necessary discrimination are often constrained to do so for our own guidance. It is the violation of the law of love involved in the exercise of a censorious disposition which alone is here condemned. And the argument against it--"that ye be not judged"--confirms this: "that your own character and actions be not pronounced upon with the like severity"; that is, at the great day. <div eID="gen25628" type="x-p"/>
entries.939bcb958f440465a69a86146382829f387b589c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13434"/><div sID="gen25629" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13434"/><hi type="bold">2. For with what judgments ye judge, ye shall be judged: and with what measure ye mete--</hi>whatever standard of judgment ye apply to others.<div eID="gen25629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25630" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">it shall be measured to you again--</hi>This proverbial maxim is used by our Lord in other connections--as in <reference osisRef="Mark.4.24">Mr 4:24</reference>, and with a slightly different application in <reference osisRef="Luke.6.38">Lu 6:38</reference>--as a great principle in the divine administration. Unkind judgment of others will be judicially returned upon ourselves, in the day when God shall judge the secrets of men by Jesus Christ. But, as in many other cases under the divine administration, such harsh judgment gets self-punished even here. For people shrink from contact with those who systematically deal out harsh judgment upon others--naturally concluding that they themselves may be the next victims--and feel impelled in self-defense, when exposed to it, to roll back upon the assailant his own censures. <div eID="gen25630" type="x-p"/>
entries.4dd1812073fe88a5685c5275efe3785db9aca327: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13435"/><div sID="gen25631" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13435"/><hi type="bold">3. And why beholdest thou the mote--</hi>"splinter," here very well rendered "mote," denoting any small fault.<div eID="gen25631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25632" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that is in thy brother's eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye?--</hi>denoting the much greater fault which we overlook in ourselves. <div eID="gen25632" type="x-p"/>
entries.cdcced3b49d7592df8c68b084179c4d2cfdeda0e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13436"/><div sID="gen25633" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13436"/>4. Or how wilt thou say to thy brother, Let me pull out the mote out of thine eye; and, behold, a beam is in thine own eye? <div eID="gen25633" type="x-p"/>
entries.be2eda3a5296f2c729e338fa049f192337b05ee4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13437"/><div sID="gen25634" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13437"/><hi type="bold">5. Thou hypocrite--</hi>"Hypocrite."<div eID="gen25634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25635" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">first cast out the beam out of thine own eye; and then shalt thou see clearly to cast out the mote out of thy brother's eye--</hi>Our Lord uses a most hyperbolical, but not unfamiliar figure, to express the monstrous inconsistency of this conduct. The "hypocrisy" which, not without indignation, He charges it with, consists in the pretense of a zealous and compassionate charity, which cannot possibly be real in one who suffers worse faults to lie uncorrected in himself. He only is fit to be a reprover of others who jealously and severely judges himself. Such persons will not only be slow to undertake the office of censor on their neighbors, but, when constrained in faithfulness to deal with them, will make it evident that they do it with reluctance and not satisfaction, with moderation and not exaggeration, with love and not harshness.<div eID="gen25635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25636" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Prostitution of Holy Things (<reference osisRef="Matt.7.6">Mt 7:6</reference>). The opposite extreme to that of censoriousness is here condemned--</hi>want of discrimination of character. <div eID="gen25636" type="x-p"/>
entries.adaa875af30a318b8d88b063600e399b44da936d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13438"/><div sID="gen25637" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13438"/><hi type="bold">6. Give not that which is holy unto the dogs--</hi>savage or snarling haters of truth and righteousness.<div eID="gen25637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25638" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither cast ye your pearls before swine--</hi>the impure or coarse, who are incapable of appreciating the priceless jewels of Christianity. In the East, dogs are wilder and more gregarious, and, feeding on carrion and garbage, are coarser and fiercer than the same animals in the West. Dogs and swine, besides being ceremonially unclean, were peculiarly repulsive to the Jews, and indeed to the ancients generally.<div eID="gen25638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25639" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lest they trample them under their feet--</hi>as swine do.<div eID="gen25639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25640" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and turn again and rend you--</hi>as dogs do. Religion is brought into contempt, and its professors insulted, when it is forced upon those who cannot value it and will not have it. But while the indiscriminately zealous have need of this caution, let us be on our guard against too readily setting our neighbors down as dogs and swine, and excusing ourselves from endeavoring to do them good on this poor plea.<div eID="gen25640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25641" type="x-p"/> Prayer (<reference osisRef="Matt.7.7-Matt.7.11">Mt 7:7-11</reference>). Enough, one might think, had been said on this subject in <reference osisRef="Matt.6.5-Matt.6.15">Mt 6:5-15</reference>. But the difficulty of the foregoing duties seems to have recalled the subject, and this gives it quite a new turn. "How shall we ever be able to carry out such precepts as these, of tender, holy, yet discriminating love?" might the humble disciple inquire. "Go to God with it," is our Lord's reply; but He expresses this with a fulness which leaves nothing to be desired, urging now not only confidence, but importunity in prayer. <div eID="gen25641" type="x-p"/>
entries.15022ea7e9b39084a11cb86c5f50b25f02d3177c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13439"/><div sID="gen25642" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13439"/><hi type="bold">7. Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you--</hi>Though there seems evidently a climax here, expressive of more and more importunity, yet each of these terms used presents what we desire of God in a different light. We ask for what we wish; we seek for what we miss; we knock for that from which we feel ourselves shut out. Answering to this threefold representation is the triple assurance of success to our believing efforts. "But ah!" might some humble disciple say, "I cannot persuade myself that I have any interest with God." To meet this, our Lord repeats the triple assurance He had just given, but in such a form as to silence every such complaint. <div eID="gen25642" type="x-p"/>
entries.12ed5a4e76423211a51084f8529dc6e856ba9f4e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13440"/><div sID="gen25643" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13440"/><hi type="bold">8. For every one that asketh receiveth; and he that seeketh findeth; and to him that knocketh it shall be opened--</hi>Of course, it is presumed that he asks aright--that is, in faith--and with an honest purpose to make use of what he receives. "If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God. But let him ask in faith, nothing wavering (undecided whether to be altogether on the Lord's side). For he that wavereth is like a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed. For let not that man think that he shall receive any thing of the Lord" (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.5-Jas.1.7">Jas 1:5-7</reference>). Hence, "Ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss, that ye may consume it upon your lusts" (<reference osisRef="Jas.4.3">Jas 4:3</reference>). <div eID="gen25643" type="x-p"/>
entries.53b77b4d1ef0231885bde3770cf8d891f241abab: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13441"/><div sID="gen25644" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13441"/><hi type="bold">9. Or what man is there of you, whom if his son ask bread--</hi>a loaf.<div eID="gen25644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25645" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">will he give him a stone?--</hi>round and smooth like such a loaf or cake as was much in use, but only to mock him. <div eID="gen25645" type="x-p"/>
entries.13158dd69c4889672ea04dbc079839795e7008b5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13442"/><div sID="gen25646" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13442"/><hi type="bold">10. Or if he ask a fish, will he give him a serpent?--</hi>like it, indeed, but only to sting him. <div eID="gen25646" type="x-p"/>
entries.211e9542c4b2f5741d7c4388d17fca7d67681ea6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13443"/><div sID="gen25647" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13443"/><hi type="bold">11. If ye then, being evil, know how to give good gifts unto your children, how much more shall your Father which is in heaven give good things to them that ask him!--</hi>Bad as our fallen nature is, the father in us is not extinguished. What a heart, then, must the Father of all fathers have towards His pleading children! In the corresponding passage in Luke (see on <reference osisRef="Luke.11.13">Lu 11:13</reference>), instead of "good things," our Lord asks whether He will not much more give the Holy Spirit to them that ask Him. At this early stage of His ministry, and before such an audience, He seems to avoid such sharp doctrinal teaching as was more accordant with His plan at the riper stage indicated in Luke, and in addressing His own disciples exclusively.<div eID="gen25647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25648" type="x-p"/> Golden Rule (<reference osisRef="Matt.7.12">Mt 7:12</reference>). <div eID="gen25648" type="x-p"/>
entries.ede3598ab83d0e4de24b126f4ee19a0bf45b6970: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13444"/><div sID="gen25649" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13444"/><hi type="bold">12. Therefore--</hi>to say all in one word.<div eID="gen25649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25650" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them--</hi>the same thing and in the same way.<div eID="gen25650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25651" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for this is the law and the prophets--</hi>"This is the substance of all relative duty; all Scripture in a nutshell." Incomparable summary! How well called "the royal law!" (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.8">Jas 2:8</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Rom.13.9">Ro 13:9</reference>). It is true that similar maxims are found floating in the writings of the cultivated Greeks and Romans, and naturally enough in the Rabbinical writings. But so expressed as it is here--in immediate connection with, and as the sum of such duties as has been just enjoined, and such principles as had been before taught--it is to be found nowhere else. And the best commentary upon this fact is, that never till our Lord came down thus to teach did men effectually and widely exemplify it in their practice. The precise sense of the maxim is best referred to common sense. It is not, of course, what--in our wayward, capricious, gasping moods--we should wish that men would do to us, that we are to hold ourselves bound to do to them; but only what--in the exercise of an impartial judgment, and putting ourselves in their place--we consider it reasonable that they should do to us, that we are to do to them.<div eID="gen25651" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.7.13-Matt.7.29">Mt 7:13-29</reference>. Conclusion and Effect of the Sermon on the Mount.</title> <div sID="gen25652" type="x-p"/> We have here the application of the whole preceding discourse.<div eID="gen25652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25653" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Conclusion of the Sermon on the Mount (<reference osisRef="Matt.7.13-Matt.7.27">Mt 7:13-27</reference>). "The righteousness of the kingdom," so amply described, both in principle and in detail, would be seen to involve self-sacrifice at every step. Multitudes would never face this. But it must be faced, else the consequences will be fatal. This would divide all within the sound of these truths into two classes: the many, who will follow the path of ease and self-indulgence--</hi>end where it might; and the few, who, bent on eternal safety above everything else, take the way that leads to it--at whatever cost. This gives occasion to the two opening verses of this application. <div eID="gen25653" type="x-p"/>
entries.f1671fafe21b5dff26c6efe95ee6b476a3300571: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13445"/><div sID="gen25654" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13445"/><hi type="bold">13. Enter ye in at the strait gate--</hi>as if hardly wide enough to admit one at all. This expresses the difficulty of the first right step in religion, involving, as it does, a triumph over all our natural inclinations. Hence the still stronger expression in Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.13.24">Lu 13:24</reference>), "Strive to enter in at the strait gate."<div eID="gen25654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25655" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for wide is the gate--</hi>easily entered.<div eID="gen25655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25656" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and broad is the way--</hi>easily trodden.<div eID="gen25656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25657" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that leadeth to destruction, and--</hi>thus lured "many there be which go in thereat." <div eID="gen25657" type="x-p"/>
entries.848925457d19d91400ba332a4c401564924b1d5d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13446"/><div sID="gen25658" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13446"/><hi type="bold">14. Because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life--</hi>In other words, the whole course is as difficult as the first step; and (so it comes to pass that).<div eID="gen25658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25659" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">few there be that find it--</hi>The recommendation of the broad way is the ease with which it is trodden and the abundance of company to be found in it. It is sailing with a fair wind and a favorable tide. The natural inclinations are not crossed, and fears of the issue, if not easily hushed, are in the long run effectually subdued. The one disadvantage of this course is its end--it "leadeth to destruction." The great Teacher says it, and says it as "One having authority." To the supposed injustice or harshness of this He never once adverts. He leaves it to be inferred that such a course righteously, naturally, necessarily so ends. But whether men see this or no, here He lays down the law of the kingdom, and leaves it with us. As to the other way, the disadvantage of it lies in its narrowness and solicitude. Its very first step involves a revolution in all our purposes and plans for life, and a surrender of all that is dear to natural inclination, while all that follows is but a repetition of the first great act of self-sacrifice. No wonder, then, that few find and few are found in it. But it has one advantage--it "leadeth unto life." Some critics take "the gate" here, not for the first, but the last step in religion; since gates seldom open into roads, but roads usually terminate in a gate, leading straight to a mansion. But as this would make our Lord's words to have a very inverted and unnatural form as they stand, it is better, with the majority of critics, to view them as we have done. But since such teaching would be as unpopular as the way itself, our Lord next forewarns His hearers that preachers of smooth things--the true heirs and representatives of the false prophets of old--would be rife enough in the new kingdom. <div eID="gen25659" type="x-p"/>
entries.36cd2a6bc79635ae47a118e9dedf3c89a7734d16: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13447"/><div sID="gen25660" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13447"/><hi type="bold">15. Beware--</hi>But beware.<div eID="gen25660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25661" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of false prophets--</hi>that is, of teachers coming as authorized expounders of the mind of God and guides to heaven. (See <reference osisRef="Acts.20.29">Ac 20:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.20.30">30</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.1">2Pe 2:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.2">2</reference>).<div eID="gen25661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25662" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which come to you in sheep's clothing--</hi>with a bland, gentle, plausible exterior; persuading you that the gate is not strait nor the way narrow, and that to teach so is illiberal and bigoted--precisely what the old prophets did (<reference osisRef="Ezek.13.1-Ezek.10.22">Eze 13:1-10, 22</reference>).<div eID="gen25662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25663" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but inwardly they are ravening wolves--</hi>bent on devouring the flock for their own ends (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.2">2Co 11:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.13-2Cor.3.15">3, 13-15</reference>). <div eID="gen25663" type="x-p"/>
entries.9b6c99a10730cf499ac5c92789e0d50e09b7b3b6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13448"/><div sID="gen25664" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13448"/><hi type="bold">16. Ye shall know them by their fruits--</hi>not their doctrines--as many of the elder interpreters and some later ones explain it--for that corresponds to the tree itself; but the practical effect of their teaching, which is the proper fruit of the tree.<div eID="gen25664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25665" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Do men gather grapes of thorns--</hi>any kind of prickly plant.<div eID="gen25665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25666" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">or figs of thistles?--</hi>a three-pronged variety. The general sense is obvious--Every tree bears its own fruit. <div eID="gen25666" type="x-p"/>
entries.cad5dd83aafce5a85ecd067c013af7fb7597d0f2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13449"/><div sID="gen25667" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13449"/>17. Even so every good tree bringeth forth good fruit: but a corrupt tree bringeth forth evil fruit. <div eID="gen25667" type="x-p"/>
entries.44cf425722d3afaa1ff90a9af3814d0da9d1cb90: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13450"/><div sID="gen25668" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13450"/><hi type="bold">18. A good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit, neither can a corrupt tree bring forth good fruit--</hi>Obvious as is the truth here expressed in different forms--that the heart determines and is the only proper interpreter of the actions of our life--no one who knows how the Church of Rome makes a merit of actions, quite apart from the motives that prompt them, and how the same tendency manifests itself from time to time even among Protestant Christians, can think it too obvious to be insisted on by the teachers of divine truth. Here follows a wholesome digression. <div eID="gen25668" type="x-p"/>
entries.9eff8e6a9cefee9b101cd67254caffd5da2b7f4e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13451"/><div sID="gen25669" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13451"/><hi type="bold">19. Every tree that bringeth not forth good fruit is hewn down, and cast into the fire--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Matt.3.10">Mt 3:10</reference>). <div eID="gen25669" type="x-p"/>
entries.954e336ce0485795400364ab5d647d218a75c52f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13452"/><div sID="gen25670" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13452"/><hi type="bold">20. Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them--</hi>that is, But the point I now press is not so much the end of such, as the means of detecting them; and this, as already said, is their fruits. The hypocrisy of teachers now leads to a solemn warning against religious hypocrisy in general. <div eID="gen25670" type="x-p"/>
entries.c7f5495c6a5c85e6ebf379f0dbdf89b3f16c65dc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13453"/><div sID="gen25671" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13453"/><hi type="bold">21. Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord--</hi>the reduplication of the title "Lord" denoting zeal in according it to Christ (see <reference osisRef="Mark.14.45">Mr 14:45</reference>). Yet our Lord claims and expects this of all His disciples, as when He washed their feet: "Ye call me Master and Lord: and ye say well; for so I am" (<reference osisRef="John.13.13">Joh 13:13</reference>).<div eID="gen25671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25672" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven--</hi>that will which it had been the great object of this discourse to set forth. Yet our Lord says warily, not "the will of your Father," but "of My Father"; thus claiming a relationship to His Father with which His disciples might not intermeddle, and which He never lets down. And He so speaks here to give authority to His asseverations. But now He rises higher still--not formally announcing Himself as the Judge, but intimating what men will say to Him, and He to them, when He sits as their final judge. <div eID="gen25672" type="x-p"/>
entries.b65d8c360cae08979d899ced528dd638a7491fec: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13454"/><div sID="gen25673" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13454"/><hi type="bold">22. Many will say to me in that day--</hi>What day? It is emphatically unnamed. But it is the day to which He had just referred, when men shall "enter" or not enter "into the kingdom of heaven." (See a similar way of speaking of "that day" in <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.12">2Ti 1:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.8">4:8</reference>).<div eID="gen25673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25674" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lord, Lord--</hi>The reiteration denotes surprise. "What, Lord? How is this? Are we to be disowned?"<div eID="gen25674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25675" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">have we not prophesied--</hi>or, "publicly taught." As one of the special gifts of the Spirit in the early Church, it has the sense of "inspired and authoritative teaching," and is ranked next to the apostleship. (See <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.28">1Co 12:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.11">Ep 4:11</reference>). In this sense it is used here, as appears from what follows.<div eID="gen25675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25676" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in thy name--</hi>or, "to thy name," and so in the two following clauses--"having reference to Thy name as the sole power in which we did it."<div eID="gen25676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25677" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and in thy name have cast out devils? and in thy name done many wonderful works--</hi>or, miracles. These are selected as three examples of the highest services rendered to the Christian cause, and through the power of Christ's own name, invoked for that purpose; He Himself, too, responding to the call. And the threefold repetition of the question, each time in the same form, expresses in the liveliest manner the astonishment of the speakers at the view now taken of them. <div eID="gen25677" type="x-p"/>
entries.c67b3ec54d77587f2dacdf3655d598bc04dff6ab: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13455"/><div sID="gen25678" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13455"/><hi type="bold">23. And then will I profess unto them--</hi>or, openly proclaim--tearing off the mask.<div eID="gen25678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25679" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I never knew you--</hi>What they claimed--intimacy with Christ--is just what He repudiates, and with a certain scornful dignity. "Our acquaintance was not broken off--there never was any."<div eID="gen25679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25680" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">depart from me--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="Matt.25.41">Mt 25:41</reference>). The connection here gives these words an awful significance. They claimed intimacy with Christ, and in the corresponding passage, <reference osisRef="Luke.13.26">Lu 13:26</reference>, are represented as having gone out and in with Him on familiar terms. "So much the worse for you," He replies: "I bore with that long enough; but now--begone!"<div eID="gen25680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25681" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye that work iniquity--</hi>not "that wrought iniquity"; for they are represented as fresh from the scenes and acts of it as they stand before the Judge. (See on the almost identical, but even more vivid and awful, description of the scene in <reference osisRef="Luke.13.24-Luke.13.27">Lu 13:24-27</reference>). That the apostle alludes to these very words in <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.19">2Ti 2:19</reference> there can hardly be any doubt--"Nevertheless the foundation of God standeth sure, having this seal, The Lord knoweth them that are His. And, Let every one that nameth the name of Christ depart from iniquity." <div eID="gen25681" type="x-p"/>
entries.7657a9d0dae0af3282bef659856212a3a337f1b9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13456"/><div sID="gen25682" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13456"/><hi type="bold">24. Therefore--</hi>to bring this discourse to a close.<div eID="gen25682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25683" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them--</hi>see <reference osisRef="Jas.1.22">Jas 1:22</reference>, which seems a plain allusion to these words; also <reference osisRef="Luke.11.28">Lu 11:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.2.13">Ro 2:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.3.7">1Jo 3:7</reference>.<div eID="gen25683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25684" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I will liken him unto a wise man--</hi>a shrewd, prudent, provident man.<div eID="gen25684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25685" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which built his house upon a rock--</hi>the rock of true discipleship, or genuine subjection to Christ. <div eID="gen25685" type="x-p"/>
entries.51ade8ecef5659937735d76f715fd4a2b1f9891a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13457"/><div sID="gen25686" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13457"/><hi type="bold">25. And the rain descended--</hi>from above.<div eID="gen25686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25687" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and the floods came--</hi>from below.<div eID="gen25687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25688" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and the winds blew--</hi>sweeping across.<div eID="gen25688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25689" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and beat upon that house--</hi>thus from every direction.<div eID="gen25689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25690" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and it fell not; for it was founded upon a rock--</hi>See <reference osisRef="1John.2.17">1Jo 2:17</reference>. <div eID="gen25690" type="x-p"/>
entries.bc5f1bbd73f1a0478675a54d3e04d407211c8474: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13458"/><div sID="gen25691" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13458"/><hi type="bold">26. And every one that heareth these sayings of mine--</hi>in the attitude of discipleship.<div eID="gen25691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25692" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and doeth them not, shall be likened unto a foolish man, which built his house upon the sand--</hi>denoting a loose foundation--that of an empty profession and mere external services. <div eID="gen25692" type="x-p"/>
entries.f6a81030293f169d675cea8a2b5b2097e32ed0dc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13459"/><div sID="gen25693" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13459"/><hi type="bold">27. And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house--</hi>struck against that house;<div eID="gen25693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25694" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and it fell: and great was the fall of it--</hi>terrible the ruin! How lively must this imagery have been to an audience accustomed to the fierceness of an Eastern tempest, and the suddenness and completeness with which it sweeps everything unsteady before it!<div eID="gen25694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25695" type="x-p"/> Effect of the Sermon on the Mount (<reference osisRef="Matt.7.28">Mt 7:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.7.29">29</reference>). <div eID="gen25695" type="x-p"/>
entries.6acdfcf4ded6b2388a49a3a625d3aca94b27af08: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13460"/><div sID="gen25696" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13460"/><hi type="bold">28. And it came to pass, when Jesus had ended these sayings, the people were astonished at his doctrine--</hi>rather, "His teaching," for the reference is to the manner of it quite as much as the matter, or rather more so. <div eID="gen25696" type="x-p"/>
entries.dff64bad387ed663a768fe05d6a64b7bdd900015: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13461"/><div sID="gen25697" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13461"/><hi type="bold">29. For he taught them as one having authority--</hi>The word "one," which our translators have here inserted, only weakens the statement.<div eID="gen25697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25698" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and not as the scribes--</hi>The consciousness of divine authority, as Lawgiver, Expounder and Judge, so beamed through His teaching, that the scribes' teaching could not but appear drivelling in such a light. <chapter eID="Matt.7"/>

entries.ee3df39df404254e11b176f64361f170e01a9d03: <div eID="gen36698" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen36699" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen36700" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen36700" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen36699" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen36701" type="x-p"/> Our Lord warns men against rash judgment and uncharitable censures, <reference osisRef="Mat.7.1-Mat.7.5">Mat 7:1-5</reference>. Shows that holy things must not be profaned, <reference osisRef="Mat.7.6">Mat 7:6</reference>; gives encouragement to fervent persevering prayer, <reference osisRef="Mat.7.7-Mat.7.11">Mat 7:7-11</reference>. Shows how men should deal with each other, <reference osisRef="Mat.7.12">Mat 7:12</reference>. Exhorts the people to enter in at the strait gate, <reference osisRef="Mat.7.13">Mat 7:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.7.14">Mat 7:14</reference>; to beware of false teachers, who are to be known by their fruits, <reference osisRef="Mat.7.15-Mat.7.20">Mat 7:15-20</reference>. Shows that no man shall be saved by his mere profession of Christianity, however specious, <reference osisRef="Mat.7.22">Mat 7:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.7.23">Mat 7:23</reference>. The parable of the wise man who built his house upon a rock, <reference osisRef="Mat.7.24">Mat 7:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.7.25">Mat 7:25</reference>. Of the foolish man who built his house, without a foundation, on the sand, <reference osisRef="Mat.7.26">Mat 7:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.7.27">Mat 7:27</reference>. Christ concludes his sermon, and the people are astonished at his doctrine, <reference osisRef="Mat.7.28">Mat 7:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.7.29">Mat 7:29</reference>. <div eID="gen36701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36702" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen36702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36703" type="x-p"/> Judge not, that ye be not judged - These exhortations are pointed against rash, harsh, and uncharitable judgments, the thinking evil, where no evil seems, and speaking of it accordingly. The Jews were highly criminal here, and yet had very excellent maxims against it, as may be seen in Schoettgen. This is one of the most important exhortations in the whole of this excellent sermon. By a secret and criminal disposition of nature, man endeavors to elevate himself above others, and, to do it more effectually, depresses them. His jealous and envious heart wishes that there may be no good quality found but in himself, that he alone may be esteemed. Such is the state of every unconverted man; and it is from this criminal disposition, that evil surmises, rash judgments, precipitate decisions, and all other unjust procedures against our neighbor, flow.
entries.960fd1ff28b1b65721ede1fa6dae26586abb3839: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen36703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36704" type="x-p"/> For with what judgment - He who is severe on others will naturally excite their severity against himself. The censures and calumnies which we have suffered are probably the just reward of those which we have dealt out to others.
entries.18aba5e1a8c3827ca0ccafb1c4290e97a41f4216: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen36704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36705" type="x-p"/> And why beholdest thou the mote - Καρφος might be translated the splinter: for splinter bears some analogy to beam, but mote does not. I should prefer this word (which has been adopted by some learned men) on the authority of Hesychius, who is a host in such matters; Καρφος, κεραια ξυλου λεπτη, Karphos is a thin piece of wood, a splinter. It often happens that the faults which we consider as of the first enormity in others are, to our own iniquities, as a chip is, when compared to a large beam. On one side, self-love blinds us to ourselves; and, on the other, envy and malice give us piercing eyes in respect of others. When we shall have as much zeal to correct ourselves, as we have inclination to reprove and correct others, we shall know our own defects better than now we know those of our neighbor. There is a caution very similar to this of our Lord given by a heathen: - <div eID="gen36705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36706" type="x-p"/> Cum tua praevideas oculis mala lippus inunctis: <div eID="gen36706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36707" type="x-p"/> Cur in amicorum vitiis tam cernis acutum, <div eID="gen36707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36708" type="x-p"/> Quam aut aquila, aut serpens Epidaurius? <div eID="gen36708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36709" type="x-p"/> Hor. Sat. lib. 1. sat. 3. l. 25-27 "When you can so readily overlook your own wickedness, why are you more clear-sighted than the eagle or serpent of Epidaurus, in spying out the failings of your friends?" <div eID="gen36709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36710" type="x-p"/> But the saying was very common among the Jews, as may be seen in Lightfoot.
entries.fc01513b0b0354a272e8574501ee8ffaed83b01e: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen36710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36711" type="x-p"/> Or how wilt thou say - That man is utterly unfit to show the way of life to others who is himself walking in the way of death.
entries.ebfdfc0cdf4298122017fa3f0ae43474e9de1e3f: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen36711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36712" type="x-p"/> Thou hypocrite - A hypocrite, who professes to be what he is not, (viz. a true Christian), is obliged, for the support of the character he has assumed, to imitate all the dispositions and actions of a Christian; consequently he must reprove sin, and endeavor to show an uncommon affection for the glory of God. Our Lord unmasks this vile pretender to saintship, and shows him that his hidden hypocrisy, covered with the garb of external sanctity, is more abominable in the sight of God than the openly professed and practised iniquity of the profligate. <div eID="gen36712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36713" type="x-p"/> In after times, the Jews made a very bad use of this saying: "I wonder," said Rabbi Zarphon, "whether there be any in this age that will suffer reproof? If one say to another, Cast out the mote out of thine eye, he is immediately ready to answer, Cast out the beam that is in thine own eye." <div eID="gen36713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36714" type="x-p"/> This proverbial mode of speech the Gloss interprets thus: "Cast out? קסים kisim, the mote, that is, the little sin, that is in thy hand: to which he answered, Cast out the great sin that is in thine. So they could not reprove, because all were sinners." See Lightfoot.
entries.aa77fd1ba4553d7c847b1137267f46c3e655f1cb: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen36714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36715" type="x-p"/> Give not that which is holy - Το αγιον, the holy or sacred thing; i.e. any thing, especially, of the sacrificial kind, which had been consecrated to God. The members of this sentence should be transposed thus: - <div eID="gen36715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36716" type="x-p"/> Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, <div eID="gen36716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36717" type="x-p"/> Lest they turn again and rend you: <div eID="gen36717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36718" type="x-p"/> Neither cast ye your pearls before swine, <div eID="gen36718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36719" type="x-p"/> Lest they trample them under their feet <div eID="gen36719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36720" type="x-p"/> The propriety of this transposition is self-evident. There are many such transpositions as these, both in sacred and profane writers. The following is very remarkable: - "I am black but comely; "As the tents of Kedar, as the curtains of Solomon." <div eID="gen36720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36721" type="x-p"/> That is, "I am black as the tents of Kedar, "Comely as the curtains of Solomon." <div eID="gen36721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36722" type="x-p"/> See many proofs of this sort of writing in Mr. Wakefield's Commentary. <div eID="gen36722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36723" type="x-p"/> As a general meaning of this passage, we may just say: "The sacrament of the Lord's supper, and other holy ordinances which are only instituted for the genuine followers of Christ, are not to be dispensed to those who are continually returning like the snarling ill-natured dog to their easily predominant sins of rash judgment, barking at and tearing the characters of others by evil speaking, back biting and slandering; nor to him who, like the swine, is frequently returning to wallow in the mud of sensual gratifications and impurities."
entries.c039c76cbd3b73535ebe03c04e348612b765c9ba: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen36723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36724" type="x-p"/> Ask - seek - knock - These three words include the ideas of want, loss, and earnestness. <div eID="gen36724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36725" type="x-p"/> Ask: turn, beggar at, the door of mercy; thou art destitute of all spiritual good, and it is God alone who can give it to thee; and thou hast no claim but what his mercy has given thee on itself. <div eID="gen36725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36726" type="x-p"/> Seek: Thou hast lost thy God, thy paradise, thy soul. - Look about thee - leave no stone unturned there is no peace, no final salvation for thee till thou get thy soul restored to the favor and image of God. <div eID="gen36726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36727" type="x-p"/> Knock: Be in earnest - be importunate: Eternity is at hand! and, if thou die in thy sins, where God is thou shalt never come. <div eID="gen36727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36728" type="x-p"/> Ask with confidence and humility. <div eID="gen36728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36729" type="x-p"/> Seek with care and application. <div eID="gen36729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36730" type="x-p"/> Knock with earnestness and perseverance.
entries.850d348894c5dbc7b0f31580bc6aad51a8cc146e: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen36730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36731" type="x-p"/> For every one that asketh receiveth - Prayer is always heard after one manner or other. No soul can pray in vain that prays as directed above. The truth and faithfulness of the Lord Jesus are pledged for its success. - Ye Shall receive - ye Shall find - it Shall be opened. These words are as strongly binding on the side of God, as thou shalt do no murder is on the side of man. Bring Christ's word, and Christ's sacrifice with thee, and not one of Heaven's blessings can be denied thee. See on <reference osisRef="Luk.11.9">Luk 11:9</reference> (note).
entries.127b9ee8066f2b66e3bbcf584ec045d5c1f45310: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen36731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36732" type="x-p"/> Or what man is there - whom if his son - Men are exhorted to come unto God, with the persuasion that he is a most gracious and compassionate Parent, who possesses all heavenly and earthly good, knows what is necessary for each of his creatures, and is infinitely ready to communicate that which they need most. <div eID="gen36732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36733" type="x-p"/> Will he give him a stone? - Will he not readily give him bread if he have it? This was a proverb in other countries; a benefit grudgingly given by an avaricious man is called by Seneca, panem lapidosum, stony bread. Hence that saying in Plautus: Altera manu, fert lapidem, panem ostentat altera. - In one hand he brings a stone, and stretches out bread in the other.
entries.1c57000b7b9fdde4e35d91305f0043c2fd4f64a8: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen36733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36734" type="x-p"/> If ye, then, being evil - Πονηροι οντες, who are radically and diabolically depraved, yet feel yourselves led, by natural affection, to give those things to your children which are necessary to support their lives, how much more will your Father who is in heaven, whose nature is infinite goodness, mercy, and grace, give good things - his grace and Spirit (πνευμα αγιον, the Holy Ghost, <reference osisRef="Luk.11.13">Luk 11:13</reference>), to them who ask him? What a picture is here given of the goodness of God! Reader, ask thy soul, could this heavenly Father reprobate to unconditional eternal damnation any creature he has made? He who can believe that he has, may believe any thing: but still God Is Love.
entries.02a41120ef70e8d2dc175aad08b433edb66da605: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen36734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36735" type="x-p"/> Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men - This is a most sublime precept, and highly worthy of the grandeur and beneficence of the just God who gave it. The general meaning of it is this: "Guided by justice and mercy, do unto all men as you would have them to do to you, were your circumstances and theirs reversed." Yet this saying may be misunderstood. "If the prisoner should ask the judge, 'whether he would be content to be hanged, were he in his case,' he would answer, 'No.' Then, says the prisoner, do as you would be done to. - Neither of them must do as private men; but the judge must do by him as they have publicly agreed: that is, both judge and prisoner have consented to a law, that if either of them steal he shall be hanged." - Selden. None but he whose heart is filled with love to God and all mankind can keep this precept, either in its spirit or letter. Self-love will feel itself sadly cramped when brought within the limits of this precept; but God hath spoken it: it is the spirit and design of the law and the prophets; the sum of all that is laid down in the Sacred Writings, relative to men's conduct toward each other. It seems as if God had written it upon the hearts of all men, for sayings of this kind may be found among all nations, Jewish, Christian, and Heathen. See many examples in Wetstein's notes.
entries.3f9fd617fb552376f7e4d56960885e7573443a5b: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen36735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36736" type="x-p"/> Enter ye in at the strait gate - Our Savior seems to allude here to the distinction between the public and private ways mentioned by the Jewish lawyers. The public roads were allowed to be sixteen cubits broad, the private ways only four. The words in the original are very emphatic: Enter in (to the kingdom of heaven) through This strait gate, δια της στενης πυλης, i.e. of doing to every one as you would he should do unto you; for this alone seems to be the strait gate which our Lord alludes to. <div eID="gen36736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36737" type="x-p"/> For wide is the gate - And very broad, ευρυχωρος, from ευρυς, broad, and χωρος, a place, a spacious roomy place, that leadeth forward, απαγουσα, into That destruction, εις την απωλειαν, meaning eternal misery; intimating, that it is much more congenial, to the revengeful, covetous heart of fallen man, to take every advantage of another, and to enrich himself at his expense, rather than to walk according to the rule laid down before, by our blessed Lord, and that acting contrary to it is the way to everlasting misery. With those who say it means repentance, and forsaking sin, I can have no controversy. That is certainly a gate, and a strait one too, through which every sinner must turn to God, in order to find salvation. But the doing to every one as we would they should do unto us, is a gate extremely strait, and very difficult, to every unregenerate mind.
entries.cb32a41db8af90f19173cb1b175ffc5ac8d8b365: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen36737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36738" type="x-p"/> Because strait is the gate - Instead of οτι because, I should prefer τι how, which reading is supported by a great majority of the best MSS., versions, and fathers. How strait is that gate! This mode of expression more forcibly points out the difficulty of the way to the kingdom. How strange is it that men should be unwilling to give up their worldly interests to secure their everlasting salvation! And yet no interest need be abandoned, but that which is produced by injustice and unkindness. Reason, as well as God, says, such people should be excluded from a place of blessedness. He who shows no mercy (and much more he who shows no justice) shall have judgment without mercy. <reference osisRef="Jam.2.13">Jam 2:13</reference>. <div eID="gen36738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36739" type="x-p"/> Few there be that find it - The strait gate, στενη πυλη, signifies literally what we call a wicket, i.e. a little door in a large gate. Gate, among the Jews, signifies, metaphorically, the entrance, introduction, or means of acquiring any thing. So they talk of the gate of repentance, the gate of prayers, and the gate of tears. When God, say they, shut the gate of paradise against Adam, He opened to him the gate of repentance. The way to the kingdom of God is made sufficiently manifest - the completest assistance is promised in the way, and the greatest encouragement to persevere to the end is held out in the everlasting Gospel. But men are so wedded to their own passions, and so determined to follow the imaginations of their own hearts, that still it may be said: There are few who find the way to heaven; fewer yet who abide any time in it; fewer still who walk in it; and fewest of all who persevere unto the end. Nothing renders this way either narrow or difficult to any person, but sin. Let all the world leave their sins, and all the world may walk abreast in this good way.
entries.2fd4ff56d3d14a568d1b585031ec05702dfb7a07: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen36739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36740" type="x-p"/> Beware of false prophets - By false prophets we are to understand teachers of erroneous doctrines, who come professing a commission from God, but whose aim is not to bring the heavenly treasure to the people, but rather to rob them of their earthly good. Teachers who preach for hire, having no motive to enter into the ministry but to get a living, as it is ominously called by some, however they may bear the garb and appearance of the innocent useful sheep, the true pastors commissioned by the Lord Jesus, or to whatever name, class or party they may belong, are, in the sight of the heart-searching God, no other than ravenous wolves, whose design is to feed themselves with the fat, and clothe themselves with the fleece, and thus ruin, instead of save, the flock.
entries.feb231e9fa87fc0b505a429675e55ad18b67aba5: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen36740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36741" type="x-p"/> Ye shall know them by their fruits - Fruits, in the Scripture and Jewish phraseology, are taken for works of any kind. "A man's works," says one, "are the tongue of his heart, and tell honestly whether he is inwardly corrupt or pure." By these works you may distinguish (επιγνωσεσθε) these ravenous wolves from true pastors. The judgment formed of a man by his general conduct is a safe one: if the judgment be not favorable to the person, that is his fault, as you have your opinion of him from his works, i.e. the confession of his own heart.
entries.f2a55c624698dad00ba1bbd1e3afd2b04b9c3654: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen36741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36742" type="x-p"/> So every good tree - As the thorn can only produce thorns, not grapes; and the thistle, not figs, but prickles; so an unregenerate heart will produce fruits of degeneracy. As we perfectly know that a good tree will not produce bad fruit, and the bad tree will not, cannot produce good fruit, so we know that the profession of godliness, while the life is ungodly, is imposture, hypocrisy, and deceit. A man cannot be a saint and a sinner at the same time. Let us remember, that as the good tree means a good heart, and the good fruit, a holy life, and that every heart is naturally vicious; so there is none but God who can pluck up the vicious tree, create a good heart, plant, cultivate, water, and make it continually fruitful in righteousness and true holiness.
entries.b2d5bb2d886f5a09d097788c3cda40ab98c0b62d: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen36742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36743" type="x-p"/> A good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit - Love to God and man is the root of the good tree; and from this principle all its fruit is found. To teach, as some have done, that a state of salvation may be consistent with the greatest crimes, (such as murder and adultery in David), or that the righteous necessarily sin in all their best works, is really to make the good tree bring forth bad fruit, and to give the lie to the Author of eternal truth.
entries.5c5fbe5d664d389d7135052799a28df78994a27d: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen36743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36744" type="x-p"/> Every tree that bringeth not forth good fruit - What a terrible sentence is this against Christless pastors, and Christless hearers! Every tree that produceth not good fruit, εκκοπτεται, is to be now cut down; the act of excision is now taking place: the curse of the Lord is even now on the head and the heart of every false teacher, and impenitent hearer.
entries.ba62d8a9a0f19a1c336478e1ee8fe4bcc0f0cd08: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen36744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36745" type="x-p"/> Wherefore by their fruits, etc. - This truth is often repeated, because our eternal interests depend so much upon it. Not to have good fruit is to have evil: there can be no innocent sterility in the invisible tree of the heart. He that brings forth no fruit, and he that brings forth bad fruit, are both only fit for the fire.
entries.8709af883ffcdb7713bdea8fca9238dcb9e4e9a4: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen36745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36746" type="x-p"/> Not every one - Ου πας, a Hebraism, say some, for no person. It is a Graecism and a Latinism too: ου παντων θεων, not All of the gods, i.e. not Any of the gods, Hom. Odyss. Z. 240. So Terence Sine omni periclo, without All danger, i.e. without Any danger. And Juvenal: Sine omni labe, without All imperfection, i.e. without Any. See more in Mr. Wakefield. The sense of this verse seems to be this: No person, by merely acknowledging my authority, believing in the Divinity of my nature, professing faith in the perfection of my righteousness, and infinite merit of my atonement, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven - shall have any part with God in glory; but he who doeth the will of my Father - he who gets the bad tree rooted up, the good tree planted, and continues to bring forth fruit to the glory and praise of God. There is a good saying among the rabbins on this subject. "A man should be as vigorous as a panther, as swift as an eagle, as fleet as a stag, and as strong as a lion, to do the will of his Creator."
entries.198cc701f4ca71606df0518e5c2212b23a8f805a: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen36746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36747" type="x-p"/> Many will say to me in that day - Εκεινη τη ημερα, in that very day, viz. the day of judgment - have we not prophesied, taught, publicly preached, in thy name; acknowledging thee to be the only Savior, and proclaiming thee as such to others; cast out demons, impure spirits, who had taken possession of the bodies of men; done many miracles, being assisted by supernatural agency to invert even the course of nature, and thus prove the truth of the doctrine we preached?
entries.89631dcbec88a00b6378a2f9cb3e2ea72287a823: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen36747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36748" type="x-p"/> Will I profess - Ομολογησω, I will fully and plainly tell them, I never knew you - I never approved of you; for so the word is used in many places, both in the Old and New Testaments. You held the truth in unrighteousness, while you preached my pure and holy doctrine; and for the sake of my own truth, and through my love to the souls of men, I blessed your preaching; but yourselves I could never esteem, because you were destitute of the spirit of my Gospel, unholy in your hearts, and unrighteous in your conduct. Alas! alas! how many preachers are there who appear prophets in their pulpits; how many writers, and other evangelical workmen, the miracles of whose labor, learning, and doctrine, we admire, who are nothing, and worse than nothing, before God, because they perform not his will, but their own? What an awful consideration, that a man of eminent gifts, whose talents are a source of public utility, should be only as a way-mark or finger-post in the way to eternal bliss, pointing out the road to others, without walking in it himself! <div eID="gen36748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36749" type="x-p"/> Depart from me - What a terrible word! What a dreadful separation! Depart from Me! from the very Jesus whom you have proclaimed in union with whom alone eternal life is to be found. For, united to Christ, all is heaven; separated from him, all is hell.
entries.03d278f151a97ab46f83faa8d201d1399d1fde90: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen36749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36750" type="x-p"/> Therefore whosoever heareth these sayings of mine - That is, the excellent doctrines laid down before in this and the two preceding chapters. There are several parables or similitudes like to this in the rabbins. I shall quote but the two following: - <div eID="gen36750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36751" type="x-p"/> Rabbi Eleasar said, "The man whose knowledge exceeds his works, to whom is he like? He is like a tree which had many branches, and only a few roots; and, when the stormy winds came, it was plucked up and eradicated. But he whose good works are greater than his knowledge, to what is he like? He is like a tree which had few branches, and many roots; so that all the winds of heaven could not move it from its place." Pirke Aboth. <div eID="gen36751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36752" type="x-p"/> Elisha, the son of Abuja, said, "The man who studies much in the law, and maintains good works, is like to a man who built a house, laying stones at the foundation, and building brick upon them; and, though many waters come against it, they cannot move it from its place. But the man who studies much in the law, and does not maintain good words, is like to a man who, in building his house, put brick at the foundation, and laid stones upon them, so that even gentle waters shall overthrow that house." Aboth Rab. Nath. <div eID="gen36752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36753" type="x-p"/> Probably our Lord had this or some parable in his eye: but how amazingly improved in passing through his hands! In our Lord's parable there is dignity, majesty, and point, which we seek for in vain in the Jewish archetype. <div eID="gen36753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36754" type="x-p"/> I will liken him unto a wise man - To a prudent man - ανδρι φρονιμω, to a prudent man, a man of sense and understanding, who, foreseeing the evil hideth himself, who proposes to himself the best end, and makes use of the proper means to accomplish it. True wisdom consists in getting the building of our salvation completed: to this end we must build on the Rock, Christ Jesus, and make the building firm, by keeping close to the maxims of his Gospel, and having our tempers and lives conformed to its word and spirit; and when, in order to this, we lean on nothing but the grace of Christ, we then build upon a solid rock.
entries.174408c33e7a17b0e3ec3581fc32721b877f2465: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen36754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36755" type="x-p"/> And the rain descended - floods came - winds blew - In Judea, and in all countries in the neighborhood of the tropics, the rain sometimes falls in great torrents, producing rivers, which sweep away the soil from the rocky hills; and the houses, which are built of brick only dried in the sun, of which there are whole villages in the east, literally melt away before those rains, and the land-floods occasioned by them. There are three general kinds of trials to which the followers of God are exposed; and to which, some think, our Lord alludes here: First, those of temporal afflictions, coming in the course of Divine Providence: these may be likened to the torrents of rain. Secondly, those which come from the passions of men, and which may be likened to the impetuous rivers. Thirdly, those which come from Satan and his angels, and which, like tempestuous whirlwinds, threaten to carry every thing before them. He alone, whose soul is built on the Rock of ages, stands all these shocks; and not only stands in, but profits by them.
entries.15a2d906535e9758a91502784982da1568e25546: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen36755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36756" type="x-p"/> And every one that heareth - and doeth them not - Was there ever a stricter system of morality delivered by God to man, than in this sermon? He who reads or hears it, and does not look to God to conform his soul and life to it, and notwithstanding is hoping to enter into the kingdom of heaven, is like the fool who built his house on the sand. When the rain, the rivers, and the winds come, his building must fall, and his soul be crushed into the nethermost pit by its ruins. Talking about Christ, his righteousness, merits, and atonement, while the person is not conformed to his word and spirit, is no other than solemn self-deception. <div eID="gen36756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36757" type="x-p"/> Let it be observed, that it is not the man who hears or believes these sayings of Christ, whose building shall stand, when the earth and its works are burnt up; but the man who Does them. <div eID="gen36757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36758" type="x-p"/> Many suppose that the law of Moses is abolished, merely because it is too strict, and impossible to be observed; and that the Gospel was brought in to liberate us from its obligations; but let all such know, that in the whole of the old covenant nothing can be found so exceedingly strict and holy as this sermon, which Christ lays down as the rule by which we are to walk. "Then, the fulfilling of these precepts is the purchase of glory." No, it is the Way only to that glory which has already been purchased by the blood of the Lamb. To him that believes, all things are possible.
entries.66f5fb6e909b4e39dcc626e15a5e62a604108527: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen36758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36759" type="x-p"/> And the rain descended, and the floods came, etc. - A fine illustration of this may be seen in the case of the fishermen in Bengal, who, in the dry season, build their huts on the beds of sand from which the rivers had retired: but when the rain sets in suddenly; as it often does, accompanied with violent northwest winds, and the waters pour down in torrents from the mountains; in one night, multitudes of these buildings are swept away, and the place where they stood is on the next morning indiscoverable.
entries.2ad0cd1b4dafcc46e0d4e8592fce9f31d809447a: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen36759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36760" type="x-p"/> The people were astonished - Οι οχλοι, the multitudes; for vast crowds attended the ministry of this most popular and faithful of all preachers. They were astonished at his doctrine. They heard the law defined in such a manner as they had never thought of before; and this sacred system of morality urged home on their consciences with such clearness and authority as they had never felt under the teaching of their scribes and Pharisees. Here is the grand difference between the teaching of scribes and Pharisees, the self-created or men-made ministers, and those whom God sends.
